items.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
items.summary: Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within PiS is a serious self-inflicted wound, complicating the right’s path back to power.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
By Aleks Szczerbiak
The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively.
Radical-right challengers
At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction.
PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party.
Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support.
Responding to declining support
At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance.
Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank.
The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values.
In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric.
The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński.
But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026
This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction.
Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment.
However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church.

A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence.
In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust.
“The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say.
🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr
— Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026
The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal.
The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges.
“Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement.
The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity.
“Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add.
“We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.”
The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law.
State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026
The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week.
The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review.
“Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges.

items.title: French triathlete wins Tallinn Ironman, Estonian 10th in record field
items.summary: French triathlete Remi Conte won the full-distance Tallinn Ironman on Saturday. The first Estonian finisher placed 10th.
items.body_text:
French triathlete wins Tallinn Ironman, Estonian 10th in record field
French triathlete Remi Conte won the full-distance Tallinn Ironman on Saturday. The first Estonian finisher placed 10th.
The event went ahead despite the windy conditions and Level 2 storm warning, with Conte completing the course in a time of eight hours and eight minutes.
"It's now been three years since I last finished an Ironman. It's all emotional, but I'm very happy," he told ERR after the race. Kristofer Kamberg was the top Estonian competitor, finishing 10th.
The race is the largest triathlon in the Baltic states and attracted a record 4,300 entrants this year, for the full triathlon on Saturday and the 70.3 half-distance on Sunday. Around 1,500 people were involved in staffing the event, whose headquarters was the Unibet Arena.
Chief organizer Ain-Alar Juhanson told ERR a total of 97 nations are represented in the event across all categories, with 1,900 people due to start the full race, almost as many competing in the 70.3 race, as well as 150 teams. "Those are numbers we have never seen here before," Juhanson added.
Lake Raku, just south of Tallinn, was used for the swimming stage for the first time.
The toughest part of the 226-kilometer race for the winner turned out to be the final discipline, the run. "The start of the swim was delayed a little because of fog. We started later. The bike was okay, a bit of wind, and I didn't get any rain at first. But it started raining at the beginning of the second lap of the run," Conte noted.
Kamberg completed the course in eight hours and 37 minutes, 29 minutes behind the winner, giving him 10th place. "It wasn't easy. In fact, it was hard the whole time. The weather was probably in our favor, even though it's raining, because it didn't get hot, and my first reaction is: damn, this really is hard," Kamberg said.
This was only his second Ironman, and he called himself a "below-average Estonian amateur" who had not put a massive emphasis on training in the run-up to the event. In a triathlon context, his level of modest training would take up about 10–12 hours a week. "I was actually a little worried about that coming here," he continued, and, as with Conte, found the run the hardest part.
"My leg muscles started giving out midway through the run, and that was really the main reason my pace dropped off as it did," Kamberg added.
The Baltics' largest triathlon festival culminates in Tallinn on Sunday with a half-distance race, where Estonians Kaidi Kivioja and Henry Räppo defend their titles. The event is already underway at the time of writing.
In the women's race, Kaidi Kivioja is looking to repeat last year's win, and her Estonian record over the full distance at the European Championships in Germany in June bodes well for that.
"You can't just look at past results and assume that anything is guaranteed this Sunday. But I'm going to go out there and give it my best," Kivioja said, noting she took on a new coach and new training regime this year.
Some of the traffic restrictions in place Saturday will remain in place on Sunday. The 70.3 race got underway at 9.00 a.m. today.

items.title: Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
items.summary: The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.
items.body_text:
Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.
Heavy rain — with some locations receiving the average monthly rainfall in the space of 24 hours — and strong winds swept across Estonia over the weekend, bringing down trees, causing power outages and disrupting ferry services.
The weather warning has been downgraded to Level 1 (yellow) in western and southern Estonia as of Sunday morning. Eastern Estonia – Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Järva, Jõgeva and Tartu counties – are now not subject to the warning and the weather map is showing green as of the time of writing.
Heavy rain is to continue over Estonia on Sunday morning, with 24-hour totals of 50–70 millimeters and up to 90 millimeters in some areas. These higher figures are roughly the same as the overall average rainfall for August, usually the wettest month, in Estonia.
Wind gusts reached as high as 30 meters per second on Saturday and the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) has been notified of fallen trees on roads and power lines.
The storm also left households without power: On Saturday evening, 3,410 households were without power according to Elektrilevi. As of 9 a.m. Sunday, that figure had fallen to around 2,600, though around half the outages were in southeastern Estonia.
Heavy rainfall of 50–100 millimeters overnight threatened Tallinn's sewage and drainage system, and Tallinna Vesi issued flood prevention advice, including clearing gutters, avoiding parking in flood-prone areas, and reducing water use during the rain.
Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, noted that during and immediately after heavy rain, the public should avoid using large amounts of water to avoid placing additional strain on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the sewer network to avoid overloading the system, and Kütt stressed people should avoid flooded basements and manholes due to electrocution and other hazards.
Ferry services were subject to cancellation during the storm but are back online as of Sunday morning. The 8.30 a.m. sailing from Rohuküla to Heltermaa (Hiiumaa) went ahead, and the 10 a.m. service in the other direction is also on schedule. No changes to the Virtsu to Kuivastu (Muhu/Saaremaa) route timetable are currently expected.
The storm also hit Latvia and Lithuania. Latvia's weather service issued a storm warning, outdoor events were canceled and roads were flooded in several places. In Riga, water accumulated beneath viaducts, disrupting traffic. According to Lithuanian media, at least one person was killed after being struck by a falling tree and over 150,000 households were left without power.
--

items.title: 2+2 traffic to be restored on Tallinn's Hipodroomi intersection by school year start
items.summary: By August 31, an additional traffic lane will be added at the Hipodroomi intersection in Tallinn, restoring two lanes of traffic in each direction instead of the current 2+1 traffic arrangement.
items.body_text:
2+2 traffic to be restored on Tallinn's Hipodroomi intersection by school year start
By August 31, an additional traffic lane will be added at the Hipodroomi intersection in Tallinn, restoring two lanes of traffic in each direction instead of the current 2+1 traffic arrangement.
According to Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, the change will ease capacity constraints at the intersection, although construction work in the area will continue and traffic arrangements will remain different from normal.
"With the start of the school year, traffic volumes will increase across Tallinn and major traffic jams may still occur at the Hipodroomi intersection during rush hour, resulting in longer travel times. Please plan your journey in advance and, where possible, use alternative routes and public transportation," Jesse said.
"At the same time, sidewalk construction will continue on Paldiski maantee between Merelahe tee and Endla tänav and some traffic lanes will also be closed. I urge drivers to please leave public transportation lanes for buses, as this will help buses keep to their schedules as much as possible and ensure that people get to work and children get to school," he added.
Jesse noted that after September 1, work will continue on the outbound section of Paldiski maantee between Endla tänav and Mooni tänav. That section is due to reopen to traffic at the end of November.
Work on the inbound section will begin early next year, with the entire project scheduled for completion by the end of August 2027.
Jesse said the new infrastructure will make getting around the area more convenient and safer. "Separated bike lanes, green islands and new lighting will be installed along Paldiski maantee and a new crossing for pedestrians and cyclists will be added at the intersection. The existing tree-lined section of Paldiski maantee will also be preserved and drivers will be able to turn left from Hipodroomi tänav toward the city center," Jesse said.
--
Editor: Aleksander Krjukov, Marcus Turovski

items.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
items.summary: Rights campaigner Abdulrahman al-Khalidi, who fled Saudi Arabia, has been held for four years and ten months in Bulgaria after the authorities claimed he was a national security threat.
items.body_text:
Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia. 
Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.
“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.
The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.
Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.
For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.
“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.
Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.
Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.
“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.
Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.
He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.
After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.
In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.
In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.
His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

items.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
items.summary: Big changes are afoot amid the heat of the summer holiday season. Our selection of Balkan Insight’s Premium stories takes a deep dive into the motives and agendas driving these changes.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
Landmark step
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.
While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.
Read more: Turkey Welcomes PKK Disarmament Law Despite Fears About Its Misuse (August 17, 2026)
Media freedoms
Fears have been expressed that Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic and his ruling party are plotting to muffle critical media voices in the country as important parliamentary and presidential elections approach. The latest bout of speculation was triggered by the registration of Pedro Vargas Santos David as the director of the companies which own most of United Group’s media outlets in Serbia.
United Group is in the process of selling its regional media empire to David’s Alpac Capital, which also owns the Euronews pan-European news network, but the deal still requires regulatory approval. Our analysis takes a look at what is going on behind the scenes and how it may impact regional media.
Read more: Serbian Media Outlets’ Management Change Sparks Suspicion Ahead of Elections (August 18, 2026)
Lobbying plans
With national elections approaching in October, the main Bosnian Croat political party, the HDZ, has signed a lobbying contract with US government relations company Mercury Public Affairs. It appears that HDZ leader Dragan Covic is seeking to emulate the success of his Bosnian Serb ally, Milorad Dodik.
But what is the agenda Covic and the HDZ are seeking to advance in Washington? Our analysis suggests that leveraging American power to ensure a better cut from lucrative energy projects and strengthening the Croatian position within Bosnia and Herzegovina may be the key goals.
Read more: Courting Trump’s Allies, Bosnian Croat Political Party Signs US Lobbying Contract (August 17, 2026)
Questionable intentions
Amid peak summer holiday season, Serbia’s Ministry of Education has unveiled proposed amendments to the law on school education. Nominally, these changes are pitched as aiming to prevent schools from being ‘misused’.
But with the education system having played a key role in the anti-corruption protests that have gripped Serbia since late 2024, critics are concerned that the real intention is to place the education system under tighter control to prevent a repeat.
Read more: Proposed Legal Changes to ‘Limit Rights’ Send Chill Through Serbian Schools (August 17, 2026)
Random violence
Migrants and activists in Bulgaria claim that on July 26, Bulgarian police deployed indiscriminate violence at the Pastrogor detention facility. Until December, the camp functioned as an open camp hosting migrants whose asylum applications were being processed.
Yet in December, it was turned into a detention facility in line with the EU’s new Pact on Asylum and Migration. Our story takes a look at what happened at the camp and how authorities are responding to the claims.

items.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
items.summary: Serbia has been battling wildfires for nearly a month without requesting EU assistance. Instead, it has turned to Russia for a firefighting aircraft, citing its greater water-carrying capacity.
items.body_text:
EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.
“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.
There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.
Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.
However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.
“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.
“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.
However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.
“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.
On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.
“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.
“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.
Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

items.summary: László Almásy with Magyarabs in the 1930s Hidden along the Nile near Wadi Halfa, in the borderlands of Egypt and Sudan, lies a remarkable community whose traditions are said to preserve the memory of a distant Hungarian past. items.body_text:
Latin American tourists are increasingly looking beyond Europe’s traditional destinations toward other regions.Continue reading
Hidden along the Nile near Wadi Halfa, in the borderlands of Egypt and Sudan, lies a remarkable community whose traditions are said to preserve the memory of a distant Hungarian past. Known as the Magyarabs, they trace their ancestry to Hungarian soldiers who were reportedly brought to Nubia in the 16th century and settled there as border guards. Centuries later, their story came to the attention of Hungarian explorer László Almásy, who encountered the community during his 1934 expedition.
László Almásy, the Hungarian explorer who inspired The English Patient, was one of the most renowned figures in Hungarian African exploration. He is credited with discovering the Zarzura Oasis and the Cave of the Swimmers, as well as mapping a significant portion of the Sahara.
He is said to have been the first European and Hungarian to encounter members of this community.
The encounter took place during a motor expedition to Nubia (southern Egypt and northern Sudan) in 1934–1935. In the memoirs of Henry Cecil Jackson, Governor of Sudan, it was noted that while traveling from Sudan toward Egypt, near Wadi Halfa, Count Almásy noticed that the local people were speaking a language reminiscent of Hungarian. After asking where they were from, he learned that they lived on the island of Magyar-narki, whose name means “the island of the Hungarians.”
Almásy described the details of this encounter—including his conversation with the Hungarian Arabs living on an island in the Nile near Vádi Halfa and with representatives of the tribe—in his book “In the Air… on the Sand…” (originally titled in Hungarian as Levegőben, homokon), published in 1937.
Almásy learned that the ancestors of the Magyars had been settled there more than 400 years earlier by Sultan Selim II as border guards. Almásy had to continue his journey to Cairo, where he received documents detailing the history of the Magyars. After his departure, Hansjoachim von der Esch continued researching the history of the Magyars in Wadi Halfa. On the island of Magyararti, he collected about 150 Hungarian words, and the people told him:
We men are descended from the Hungarian people; nothing about our past has ever been recorded in books, but we have preserved our history and still know very well today where we came from.”
Based on his literary research, Esch discovered that Sultan Selim I invaded Egypt in 1517 and brought captive men from Slavonia, Syrmia, Transylvania, and Bosnia, who found a home there after the fighting ended.
Their leader, Ibrahim al-Magyari—that is, Ábrahám Magyar—remained there with 20–25 cavalrymen, and they married local women. From this union, Ibrahim al-Magyari had a son named Musa, who also married a local girl, and the Hungarian tribe of Wadi Halfa is said to trace its origins to them. The population of the Magyars is estimated at 30,000–40,000.
The broader historical context is also notable: in 1516, Gábor Pécsváradi, a Franciscan monk, personally spoke with Hungarians serving in the Turkish army passing through Jerusalem, which he also recounted in a letter addressed to János Bánffy, the royal cupbearer. The monk spent 33 months in the Holy Land and recounted his experiences in a book titled Journey to Jerusalem.
The next Hungarian expedition reached the village of the Magyars in 1965.
István Fodor, the distinguished Arabist and interpreter, spent several months in Wadi Halfa during the flooding that preceded the construction of the Aswan High Dam. He researched the history, behavior, customs, and culture of the Magyar people, as well as their attitudes toward Hungarians and their Hungarian heritage.
In addition, he collected proverbs such as “Ál-Mágyárí lá jiszálli fíl-meszgyid,” meaning “A Magyar does not pray in the mosque.” This saying dates back to the time when the Magyars were still Christians. But here is another proverb: “Rá’sz el-m

items.body_text:
The world-famous chef's first Central European restaurant brings premium grilled cuisine and global culinary standards to the capital.Continue reading
A restaurant called Budapest Street Food has opened in the Lebanese city of Byblos, serving classic Hungarian dishes such as lángos (fried dough) with garlic and sour cream and giant schnitzel. The restaurant is run by a Hungarian-Lebanese family, who hope to introduce the Lebanese public to Hungarian cuisine and culture, while also creating a little piece of Hungary for the local community living here.
The story of Budapest Street Food began quite simply. The pair first sold kürtőskalács (chimney cake) at an international exhibition because they wanted to give people a little taste of Hungarian culture. The kürtőskalács proved to be a huge hit, therefore they started selling it at different festivals and events.
A bejegyzés megtekintése az Instagramon
What began as a small stand eventually grew into Budapest Street Food, Lebanon’s first and only Hungarian restaurant.
The restaurant officially opened on July 11. The opening was attended by the Ambassador of Hungary to Lebanon, the Embassy of Hungary in Beirut and the Hungarian community in Lebanon.
The restaurant offers a broad selection of Hungarian cuisine: sweet and savory dishes, as well as traditional Hungarian beverages.
From crispy lángos and delicious Kürtőskalács to hearty goulash, Hungarian burgers made with a patty of two mini lángos, and palacsinta (Hungarian crepes), the restaurant offers something to every taste.
Byblos has long been a crossroads of different cultures, religions and traditions. With its deep Christian heritage and its place at the heart of Lebanon’s Christian history, the city has welcomed influences from many parts of the world over the centuries. Budapest Street Food adds a new chapter to this long story of cultural exchange, bringing Hungarian traditions and flavors to a city where different communities have continued to meet and coexist.
Via Instagram; Featured photo: Pexels

items.title: Roman-Era Statue Discovered in the Danube Near Dunaújváros
items.summary: A Roman-era statue was discovered on Monday by employees of Dunai Industrial Diving Ltd. during a search in a section of the Danube that is difficult to dive in, FEOL reported. Additional assistance was needed to recover the artifact, which weighed several hundred kilograms; members of the Pentele Volunteer Fire Department also assisted in the […] The post Roman-Era Statue Discovered in the Danube Near Dunaújváros appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The British naval mine, exposed by unusually low water levels near Kisoroszi, was safely removed by Hungarian bomb disposal experts.Continue reading
A Roman-era statue was discovered on Monday by employees of Dunai Industrial Diving Ltd. during a search in a section of the Danube that is difficult to dive in, FEOL reported. Additional assistance was needed to recover the artifact, which weighed several hundred kilograms; members of the Pentele Volunteer Fire Department also assisted in the effort.
This latest discovery is particularly significant because the statue is almost perfectly preserved. In recent weeks, however, several other significant Roman-era artifacts have been unearthed from previously submerged sections of the Danube. In addition to experts from the Intercisa Museum, local residents and volunteers also participated in the search for the artifacts.
The Roman-era statue, which had been hidden in the depths of the Danube, was almost completely intact.
In early August, a Roman altar stone dedicated to Jupiter was discovered, which was soon reported by international archaeological publications. This was followed by the discovery of additional carved stones:
a fragment of a limestone slab was unearthed, along with a heavily weathered altar fragment that experts believe was dedicated to Deus Sol, the sun god.
A particularly striking find is a Roman-era stone fragment richly decorated with grape clusters, vines, and leaves. Recently, a piece of a tombstone was also discovered, on which traces of the original green paint still remain.
From the inscription, it was determined that the tombstone was commissioned by a man named Marcus Aurelius for himself and, presumably, his family.
The abundance of artifacts is no coincidence: the Roman military camp of Intercisa and the civilian settlement that developed around it were located in the Dunaújváros (central Hungary) area. Founded in the first century, the settlement flourished from the end of the second century until the barbarian destruction around 259–260, though its garrison remained in place until the early fifth century. Archaeological excavations in the area began as early as the late 19th century.
A significant portion of the Intercisa Museum’s collection consists of artifacts belonging to the former settlement’s inhabitants, and the current extremely low water level of the Danube has made numerous new artifacts—previously hidden beneath the water—accessible.
Via FEOL, Magyar Nemzet; Featured photo: Facebook/Intercisa Múzeum

items.title: Rossz stadion képe került rá a Sydney-ben rendezett maraton érmeire
items.summary: A szervezők beletörődtek a hibába, szerintük az érem így még egyedibb.
items.body_text:
Rossz stadion képe került rá a Sydney-ben rendezett maraton érmeire
Nem mindennapi hiba történt a Sydney-ben rendezett maratonon: véletlenül a résztvevők érmeire egy német stadion képe került rá a versenynek otthont adó stadion helyett – írja a BBC.
A rendezvény hivatalos közösségi média-oldala a hét elején nyilvánosságra hozta az idei érem tervét, amelyen tévesen a német Münchenben található Allianz Aréna volt látható a sydney-i Allianz Stadion helyett.
A Sydney-i Maraton szóvivője a BBC-nek azt mondta: sajnálatos hiba történt.
A kétoldalas éremre Sydney jellegzetes nevezetességei kerültek, köztük az Operaház és a Harbour Bridge. A közösségi médiában a felhasználók vették észre, hogy a medálra vésett stadion alakja nem pontosan úgy néz ki, ahogyan kellene.
A Sydney-i Maraton szervezői megerősítették, hogy a futók olyan medált kapnak, amelyen a helytelen város stadionja látható, de a jelek szerint egész viccesen fogták fel a helyzetet, azt mondták: „Gyönyörű érem, és most már egy kicsit még egyedibb is.”

items.title: Öt tizenéves fiatal és két bevetésen lévő rendőr halt meg egy angliai autóbalesetben
items.summary: A fiatalok autója az ütközés előtt hirtelen áttért a szemközti sávba.
items.body_text:
Öt tizenéves fiatal és két bevetésen lévő rendőr halt meg egy angliai autóbalesetben
Hét ember, köztük két rendőr életét vesztette szombaton egy autóbalesetben Anglia északkeleti részén, miután a főútvonalon egy, a forgalommal szemben haladó autó összeütközött egy éppen bevetésen lévő rendőröket szállító autóval – írja a helyi rendőrség közlése alapján a BBC. A személyautóban ülő öt tizenéves fiatal és a két rendőr a helyszínen meghalt.
A clevelandi rendőrség szerint az eset helyi idő szerint hajnali fél 4-kor történt Middlesbrough-tól keletre, a South Bank környékén. Azóta azonosították a személyautó, egy Volkswagen Passat utasait, a BBC értesülése szerint mint az öten a tizenéves koruk végén jártak. A hatóságok felvették a kapcsolatot a családjaikkal.
Andy Burnham miniszterelnök a baleset után egy rövid nyilatkozatot adott ki, amelyben kifejezte szomorúságát az eset miatt.
A közelmúltban Dublin közelében is történt két hasonló baleset, az egyik frontális ütközésben öt ember vesztette életét. Írország rendőrfőnöke a héten arra figyelmeztetett, hogy egyes fiatalok a közösségi média lájkszerzései miatt „rossz irányban haladnak az autópályán”.

items.title: Az EU helikoptereket és tűzoltókat küld Szerbiába, egy természetvédelmi területen tombol erdőtűz
items.summary: A július végén kezdődött tűz eddig több ezer hektár fenyőerdőt perzselt fel.
items.body_text:
Az EU helikoptereket és tűzoltókat küld Szerbiába, egy természetvédelmi területen tombol erdőtűz
Az EU helikoptereket és tűzoltókat küld Szerbiába az erdőtüzek miatt – írja a Reuters.
Szerbia északkeleti részén, a Delibláti-homokpusztán tombol hatalmas erdőtűz. A július végén kezdődött tűz eddig több ezer hektár fenyőerdőt perzselt fel a különleges természetvédelmi területen. A terület mintegy 80 km-re van a fővárostól, Belgrádtól, de Szerbia hetek óta nem tudja megfékezni a lángokat.
Luka Čaušić, a szerb Vészhelyzeti Hivatal vezetője azt mondta: Romániából, Szlovákiából és a Csehországból négy Black Hawk tűzoltóhelikopter, Németországból 55 tűzoltó és 24 jármű, Romániából pedig 69 tűzoltó és 15 jármű érkezik.
Szerbia nem tagja az EU-nak, de a polgári védelmi mechanizmus keretében hozzáférhet az EU sürgősségi segítségéhez.
Ezen a nyáron Belgrád egy tűzoltó helikoptert és egy sürgősségi bevetési csapatot küldött Spanyolországba, hogy segítsen az országnak a bozóttüzek leküzdésében, miután az Európában többször is kitört tűzvészek kimerítették az EU erőforrásait.
Čaušić szerint szombatra bár stabilizálódott a helyzet a Delibláti-homokpusztán, de az előrejelzett erős szél miatt továbbra sem múlt el a veszély. A hatóságok elsődleges célja a környező települések és az emberéletek védelme.
A leégett területek nagysága idén is messze meghaladja a sokévi átlagot az Európai Unióban. Múlt hónapban főként Spanyolországban és Franciaországban voltak nagy erdőtüzek, de például Horvátországban is sérültek meg magyar turisták a helyi tüzekben.

items.body_text:
More Czech Companies Test Four-Day Work Weeks Despite Political Resistance
Prague Morning
A growing number of companies in the Czech Republic are experimenting with a four-day working week, with some reporting higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction.
But politicians remain reluctant to make the arrangement a standard option across the country.
Under the model, employees work four days instead of five while keeping their full salaries. Companies that have introduced the system say workers can maintain their output while having more time to rest.
At Trinity Group, the arrangement has been in place for five years. Jan Hanulík, the company’s product and marketing director, said productivity had risen despite employees working one day less each week.
“Although we have one working day less, productivity has increased,” Hanulík said, adding that the company’s results have roughly doubled since the system was introduced.
A survey cited in the report found that around 70 percent of employees in the Czech Republic would welcome a four-day working week.
Politicians remain cautious
The idea has already been adopted in different forms elsewhere in Europe. In Belgium, for example, employees can request to work their weekly hours over four days rather than five. The system therefore does not necessarily mean fewer working hours.
Czech politicians, however, argue that a single system would not work across all sectors.
Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka of ANO said a legally mandated four-day week could create problems in areas already facing staff shortages, including social services and health care.
SPD lawmaker Lucie Šafránková also said the working week should reflect the conditions of individual professions and employers rather than follow one nationwide rule.
Czech companies are already experimenting
Several companies have introduced or tested four-day schedules, including SAB Finance, Phonexia, Sherpas, Digiskills and Café Eternity.
Not every experiment has lasted. The Cognito agency eventually returned to a traditional five-day working week after testing the shorter schedule.

items.body_text:
Foreign Workers Now Make Up 22% of Czech Employees
Prague Morning
Foreign workers accounted for around 22% of all employees in the Czech Republic at the end of 2025, according to data from the Czech National Bank (ČNB).
Their number has nearly tripled over the past decade, rising from about 323,000 in 2015 to 935,000 last year.
The increase has significantly changed the makeup of the Czech labor market. Foreign workers represented roughly 8% of all employees in 2015. By the end of 2025, their share had reached 22%.
Ukrainians made up the largest group of foreign employees, with approximately 358,000 working in Czechia at the end of last year. Slovaks were the second-largest group, numbering almost 230,000.
The Czech labor market has also seen increasing numbers of workers from other countries outside the European Union, including the Philippines and India.
Foreign workers are particularly important in several sectors, including manufacturing, construction, retail, transport and hospitality.
Their presence is most pronounced in accommodation, food services and hospitality. Foreign nationals accounted for more than half of all employees in the sector at the end of 2025.
The figures should, however, be interpreted with some caution when comparing individual industries. The CNB notes that employment agencies can distort the sectoral breakdown.
Workers employed through agencies are recorded in official statistics under administrative and support services, even when their actual jobs are in manufacturing, construction, logistics or other industries.

Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
Prague Morning
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.
The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.
The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.
Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.
The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.
Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.
Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.
Tesco faces questions over its future
The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.
According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.
Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

Harvard Georgian Studies Program Closes After Tbilisi Does Not Extend Funding
The program on Georgian Studies at Harvard University in the U.S., launched in 2022 within the Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies with the backing of the Georgian government, has closed after the Georgian Education Ministry refused to extend funding.
The Ministry cited the university’s failure to submit an “agreed program” about the project’s future as the reason for the refusal to approve the extension. Natia Chankvetadze, the program’s latest head, however, says no feedback was received from the ministry on the extension proposal, and suggested the absence of “political will” may be the true reason.
The program, with a mission to become a “leading hub” for Georgian studies outside Georgia, was first inaugurated by then-Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili in September 2021, and launched in 2022, covering teaching, research, and exchanges focused on Georgian language, history, politics, and culture, among others.
It was initially headed by Professor Stephen Jones, a longtime scholar of Georgian history and politics, before Dr. Natia Chankvetadze, a peacebuilding scholar and practitioner, assumed leadership in late August 2024.
Reports about the program’s closure emerged on August 21, with observers – including former program fellow Beka Kobakhidze – alleging that the decision stemmed from Tbilisi’s dissatisfaction with the political stances of Harvard academics, including its initial head, Stephen Jones.
Ministry Cites Absence of ‘Agreed’ Program
Commenting on initial reports about the project’s closure, the Georgian Education Ministry said on August 22 that the funding extension could not be granted because Harvard had failed to submit an “agreed program” for the project’s future.
The ministry said it “asked Harvard to provide a report on the work completed and a concrete vision for the program’s further development,” but “the program’s further extention could not be agreed because, for the launch of the new phase, no agreed program has been submitted to the ministry which would define specific activities, a budget, an implementation timeline, and measurable outcomes.”
According to the ministry, the decision not to extend the project was based “on the efficient and accountable management of state resources and the existence of the programmatic and financial framework required to launch a new phase.” It “does not mean a refusal of academic cooperation with Harvard.”
The Ministry argued that it had expressed readiness for continued cooperation as part of the program and had allocated funding, while extending funding several times, including till March 31, 2025, “to allow the program to complete remaining activities and present the relevant reports.” It also pointed to the readiness to carry out joint activities “consistent with the goals and purpose set out in the contract” after the program’s closure, noting that Harvard can still direct the funds for the program objectives “based on the submission of financial reports and documents.”
The ministry “remains ready to consider future cooperation with Harvard on the basis of clearly defined objectives, an agreed budget, an implementation timeline, and measurable outcomes,” the statement said.
Program Head Points to Lack of ‘Political Will’, No Feedback From Ministry
Speaking to Civil.ge, Natia Chankvetadze, who headed the program until late June 2026, suggested that a lack of political will may have been the real reason behind the ministry’s decision, noting that the authorities did not provide feedback on the extension proposal submitted last year.
“I think that, simply, there is no longer a political will from the ministry to extend this program rather than the reasons the Ministry cited, because they had received both the reports and the vision for the further development,” Chankvetadze said.

UN Security Council Members Condemn Russia’s Continued Occupation of Georgian Territories on August War Anniversary
Several members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) condemned Russia’s continued occupation of Georgia’s Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia regions on August 20, calling the 2008 Russo-Georgian war the beginning of Moscow’s “more aggressive stance towards its neighbors.”
The UNSC held a closed meeting on August 20 to discuss the situation in the Russia-occupied Georgian regions and the Russo-Georgian conflict, marking the 18th anniversary of the August 2008 war. According to the Georgian Foreign Ministry, Mohamed Khaled Khiari, Assistant Secretary-General for the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific, “briefed Council members on the latest developments on the ground and provided an update on the Geneva International Discussions.”
Following the meeting, representatives of UNSC members – Latvia, Denmark, France, Greece, and the United Kingdom, along with incoming Council members Austria and Portugal, issued a joint statement to the media. Deputy Permanent Representative of Latvia Oļegs Iļģis delivered the statement.
Statement in Detail
“Eighteen years have passed since Russia’s aggression and subsequent illegal occupation of Georgia’s sovereign territories of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia regions,” Iļģis said.
“The Russian invasion of Georgia in August 2008 demonstrated the start of Russia’s more aggressive stance towards its neighbors. Russia has continued down this path with its unprovoked and unjustified aggression against Ukraine and reckless and dangerous actions against its neighbors.”
The signatories reaffirmed their support for Georgia’s independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, condemning Russia’s “brutal invasion and continued illegal military presence in contravention of the UN Charter and exercising of effective control and taking steps toward annexation of the two Georgian regions.”
The statement cited the so-called “Treaty on Deepening Allied Cooperation” signed in May by Russian President Vladimir Putin and Alan Gagloev, the de facto leader of Tskhinvali/South Ossetia at the time, as well as the appointment of “a Russian citizen,” apparently referring to Marat Kambolov, as the de facto leader of Georgia’s sovereign territory, “transferring strategically important parts of Georgian territory and infrastructure to Russia and conducting illegal so-called elections.”

The countries reiterated their condemnation of Russia’s “continuous provocations, violations of international law and militarization” of the two occupied regions, pointing to “restrictions of freedom of movement, unlawful detentions and abductions of the local population, discrimination against ethnic Georgians, prohibition of education in their language, deliberate damage to Georgian cultural heritage,” as well as “erecting barbed wire fences and establishing unauthorized flights, railway and naval connections between Russia and Abkhazia region.”

items.body_text:
Tskhinvali to Expand Operation of Akhalgori, Java Crossing Points
Two crossing points along the occupation line between the occupied Tskhinvali/South Ossetia region and Tbilisi-controlled territory will operate more frequently, while close relatives of residents of certain settlements in the Akhalgori and Java districts will have simplified entry procedures, the Tskhinvali-based Res news agency reported on August 20.
According to the report, the plans were announced after a meeting of the region’s so-called “Security Council,” with de facto acting President Marat Kambolov saying residents had repeatedly raised the issue of “border crossing” to address family and everyday needs.
Kambolov said he had instructed the region’s so-called security and interior agencies to work on the issue, while stressing that the security of residents of areas close to the occupation line would remain an “unconditional” priority.
Since August 2022, residents could cross the occupation line from the 20th to the 30th of each month. Under the planned changes:
- The so-called Mosabruni (Odzisi) crossing point will operate four days a week — Thursday through Sunday — from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. It connects the predominantly ethnic Georgian Akhalgori district with Tbilisi-controlled Mtskheta Municipality.
- The so-called Perevi crossing point will operate three days a week — Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays — also from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. It connects the occupied Java district with Tbilisi-administered Sachkhere Municipality.
In addition, “the procedure for entry and temporary stay will be simplified for close relatives” of residents of certain settlements in the Akhalgori and Java districts.
The changes will take effect after the de facto government adopts a corresponding resolution.

items.title: Makhachkala woman fined $6,000 for $6 donation to Navalny’s foundation in 2021
items.summary: Aleksei Navalny’s foundation was designated extremist by the Russian government.
items.body_text:
A court in Makhachkala has fined an unnamed local woman ₽500,000 ($6,000) for transferring ₽500 ($6) to the late opposition figure Aleksei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK). She was found guilty on charges of funding extremism.
The organisation has been designated as extremist and terrorist by the Russian authorities and has been banned and liquidated.
In addition to the fine, the court ordered the ₽500 she had transferred to be confiscated and paid into state coffers.
According to the case materials, in August 2021 the woman transferred ₽500 to the FBK after following links on the organisation’s website. Investigators and the court concluded that she knew the FBK had been designated an extremist organisation. In court, the woman ‘fully admitted her guilt and expressed remorse’.
The court’s press service did not disclose the defendant’s name. However, according to the court database, the most recent case heard by Leninsky District Court in Makhachkala under this article was brought against Nazaket Gadzhibekova. The case was registered with the court on 20 April and the verdict was handed down on 18 August.
Gadzhibekova is included on Russia’s list of terrorists and extremists. According to the list, she is 47 years old and was born in the village of Kala in Rutul District in south-western Daghestan.
The FBK was designated an extremist organisation and banned in Russia in 2021. In June of that year, the Moscow City Court upheld a prosecutor’s request to designate the FBK and organisations associated with it as extremist. Donations to the FBK subsequently became grounds for criminal cases under the law on financing extremist activity.
In November 2025, a 26-year-old woman from Syria was fined ₽400,000 ($5,000) by a court in Nalchik for transferring ₽900 ($11) to the FBK. The woman said the payment had been made accidentally. According to her, she had been buying airline tickets to Turkey and may have clicked on a link without realising that she was transferring money to the FBK.
In Krasnodar in April 2025, 36-year-old Sergei Anosov was fined ₽600,000 ($7,200). According to investigators, after the FBK was designated an extremist organisation in August 2021, he set up monthly donations of ₽300 ($4) and transferred a total of ₽2,100 ($21) to the foundation by January 2022. Anosov pleaded guilty and expressed remorse.
Another man from Krasnodar, Dmitry Dyba, received a harsher sentence. In May 2025, he was sentenced to 18 months of compulsory labour for making seven transfers to the FBK totalling ₽1,050 ($12). The Krasnodar Regional Court later overturned the verdict and sent the case back for a retrial. In March 2026, following the retrial, Dyba was fined ₽300,000 ($3,600).
In the Stavropol region in January 2026, 48-year-old Konstantin Bernatov, a native of Makhachkala, was sentenced to three years in prison for making a donation to the FBK. The amount of the transfer was not disclosed. According to the prosecution, Bernatov found information about a fundraising campaign online and transferred money despite knowing that the organisation had been banned.
According to the human rights centre Memorial, at least 142 people have been accused of financing extremism over donations to the FBK, while information about new defendants in such cases continues to emerge.

items.title: Former Georgian PM Gharibashvili says state hinted at father’s arrest in third prison letter
items.summary: Despite claiming he was blackmailed, Gharibashvili stressed he remained loyal to Georgian Dream.
items.body_text:
In his latest letter from prison, Georgia’s former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili claimed that his colleagues from the ruling Georgian Dream party had twice hinted at the arrest of his father. He has also accused the party of organising a ‘dishonest and defamatory campaign’ against him.
This is the latest in a series of letters written by Gharibashvili from prison, the first claiming that he was pressured to confess to a corruption crime he did not commit on the instructions of Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili.
In his second letter, he claimed he received those instructions from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze.
Mdinaradze, meanwhile, has accused Gharibashvili of making false claims and said he would not attack the imprisoned former prime minister because of his situation in prison. Mdinaradze has also said that he and other government representatives have opposed corruption and are ready to face accusations.
‘I have heard the comments of government representatives, the false and slanderous statements of their experts. I watch the unbridled propaganda on television and social media’, Gharibashvili wrote on Thursday.
He then directly accused Mdinaradze of lying, saying: ‘If he does not want to harm innocent people, let him stop spreading lies and take full responsibility’.
Gharibashvili addressed the government directly in the letter, accusing it of setting him up with what he called a ‘dirty provocation’ and an ‘inhumane trap’.
He claimed that authorities had raided the homes of his family members and said he had endured the situation in silence because of his long-standing relationship with Ivanishvili.
‘I have endured all this terrible pain and tragedy, all with patience and silence, in my heart, because of my 20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili’, Gharibashvili wrote.
He also said he had endured the situation because of what he described as his loyalty to his ‘political family’, team, and country.
He has also claimed that a specific group within the Georgian Dream team had turned against him because of ‘envy, fears, and suspicions’.
Gharibashvili then returned to his earlier allegation that he had been pressured to confess to corruption.
He claimed that the government had approached him in prison and demanded that he admit to corruption in order to eliminate what he described as a ‘one percent risk’ that he would return to politics.
He said this pressure was accompanied by ‘immoral blackmail’ and claimed that authorities had again hinted at arresting his father.
‘This is the second time you have hinted at the arrest of my 75-year-old father’, he wrote.
Gharibashvili did not provide further details about the alleged threat or identify who he claimed had made it.
He also accused the government of trying to portray him as a traitor to Georgia, Georgian Dream, and Ivanishvili.
‘You are trying in vain and feebly to make me a traitor to the country, the team, and Bidzina Ivanishvili’, he wrote.
He warned government officials and their supporters to ‘be careful’, saying they would eventually regret their statements about him.
Gharibashvili ended the letter by repeating that he was not seeking a confrontation with the government.
‘I am not fighting anyone and I am not fighting against anyone; I am only defending myself and my family’, he wrote.
Georgian Dream officials have rejected or declined to comment on Gharibashvili’s previous claims. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said on Monday that Gharibashvili’s claims were a matter for law enforcement, adding that a court had already issued a verdict in his case. Kobakhidze also described Gharibashvili’s previous statement as ‘very problematic’, but declined to comment further, citing Gharibashvili’s former position as prime minister.

items.title: Georgian petrol company owner detained for price gouging in Marneuli
items.summary: The man has been accused of overcharging for petrol and ‘intimidating’ the locals of a village in Marneuli.
items.body_text:
Georgian authorities have detained the head of Marneuli’s Mamed Gas, Nariman Allahverdiyev, after failing to appear in court over a financial dispute with the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC). Azerbaijan’s state-run energy company SOCAR, which supplied Alakherdov with gas, had revoked his company’s distribution license in late July.
According to the local media outlet, Radio Marneuli, the main reason for the dispute was the petrol tariff price. Allahverdiyev was demanding ₾0.57 ($0.22) per litre, which is higher than the ₾0.47 ($0.18) tariff set by GNERC.
SOCAR, which operates a network of petrol stations in Georgia, issued a statement on social media saying Allahverdiyev was not paying for the subsidised petrol and accumulated around hundreds of thousands of lari in debt. It additionally claimed he continued selling petrol in the village of Kizilajlo in Marneuli, despite SOCAR suspending his distribution license.
SOCAR Georgia Gas also accused Mamed Gas of continuing its operations in the village despite the cancellation of its license and arbitrarily suspending gas supply to individual subscribers.
‘Mamed Gas LLC continues to engage in illegal actions and interrupts individual gas supply in Kizilajlo’, SOCAR said, claiming the company ‘continues to provoke, intimidate, and mislead the population’.
Allahverdiyev is under investigation under charges of illegal entrepreneurial activity, and if found guilty could face a fine or up to three years in prison.

items.title: PM's party takes harder line on immigration as election season approaches
items.summary: Petteri Orpo's National Coalition Party is drafting a policy programme that would call for stricter legislation on work-based immigration, family reunification and asylum seekers.
items.body_text:
The National Coalition Party (NCP), led by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, is currently drafting a new policy programme that would significantly tighten Finland's immigration laws.
NCP MP Atte Kaleva, who is leading the party's preparation of the programme, told Yle that Finland should be more strict about who receives residence permits.
"Economically burdensome immigration should be minimised, and immigration that benefits the national economy should be strengthened and encouraged," Kaleva said.
He further explained that the NCP's basic principle in this respect is that immigrants should have a job when they arrive in Finland, and they should remain in employment throughout their time in the country.
A tougher line
Aside from an emphasis on employment, the NCP also wants to target family reunification with its new proposals.
Family reunification refers to the practice of someone living legally in Finland applying for residence permits for their family members to join them. Under current Finnish legislation, a prerequisite for family reunification is generally that the applicant can financially support the family members they are bringing to Finland.
Another focus for the NCP will be humanitarian immigration, meaning the granting of international protection to asylum seekers or to people who arrive in Finland as quota refugees.
Finland's current laws on humanitarian immigration are vulnerable to hybrid influencing tactics by hostile states, according to Kaleva, such as the suspicions in late 2023 that Russia was funnelling large groups of migrants to eastern border checkpoints to put pressure on Finnish authorities.
"The asylum-seeking channel no longer serves the purpose for which it was created. The core idea of the National Coalition Party's immigration paper is to shift to immigration through employment," Kaleva said.
The programme paper, which will inform the party's policies ahead of next year's parliamentary elections, is due to be completed in early September.
The hot-button issue
The NCP's announcement of its plans comes in the wake of Finland's main opposition party, the Social Democrats (SDP), proposing a tougher line on integration and segregation in a policy paper published last week.
The paper called for immigrants to commit to "the core values and norms of Finnish society" and abandon "incompatible practices from their countries of origin".
The move has been seen as a significant turning point in the SDP's rhetoric on immigration, and it suggests that immigration will be a hot-button topic ahead of next spring's elections.
Kaleva said he approves of the SDP's apparent policy change.
"These ideas are going in the right direction, and if the policy paper indicates a genuine change of heart by the Social Democrats, it's only welcome. I was pleased to see it," Kaleva said.

items.title: Finland set for a damp weekend
items.summary: Unusually heavy rainfall, particularly in northern Finland, has already caused flooding, with more rain expected towards the end of the week.
items.body_text:
Changeable weather is expected across Finland over the coming weekend.
On Friday, southern and central Finland will be mostly dry and sunny. Localised showers and thunderstorms will develop in western parts of the country during the afternoon and evening.
A relatively narrow band of rain will remain around Oulu, while areas further north will stay mostly dry but largely cloudy.
Heavy rainfall this week has already caused flash flooding in northern Finland. Water levels are exceptionally high for this time of year in several rivers in Northern Ostrobothnia and Lapland.
According to the Finnish Meteorological Institute's 30-day weather data, it has rained almost every day this month in Oulu. Flood and rain warnings have been issued for more than 20 municipalities in Northern Ostrobothnia.
Cloud cover will increase slightly on Saturday, and there will be scattered showers in some areas, but most of the country will remain dry.
A strong low-pressure system is expected to move in from the south on Saturday evening and Sunday, bringing heavy rain to eastern and southeastern Finland. Winds will also strengthen considerably.

items.title: Thousands expected at Sweden climate demo as election looms
items.summary: Around 10,000 people are expected to turn out for a climate demonstration in Stockholm on Sunday, according to Swedish police and organisers, just weeks ahead of a general election where the issue is among voters' top concerns.
items.body_text:
Since taking power in 2022, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing government, backed by the populist Sweden Democrats party, has cut petrol taxes and reduced requirements for petrol suppliers to add low-carbon alternatives to their mix.
Experts both in Sweden and abroad have repeatedly warned that the government's climate policy jeopardises the country's emissions-cutting goals -- to reduce CO2 from transport by 70 percent from 2010 levels by 2030, and to achieve net-zero emissions by 2045.
Kristersson's administration has notably rejected a government-appointed commission's recommendations on ways to meet the 2030 target, which included phasing out fossil fuels by hiking taxes on petrol and diesel.
"The climate crisis is very real, and it is here," said Beatrice Rindevall, head of the Swedish Society for Nature Conservation, which is co-organising Sunday's demonstration.
"It is time to put in place a climate policy that reduces emissions right now," she added in a statement, pointing to this summer's devastating heatwaves in Europe.
Swedes go to the polls to elect a new parliament on September 13, with the right-wing bloc trailing in opinion polls.
More than 200 non-governmental organisations and associations are expected to take part in Sunday's march, which is due to start at 1:00 pm (1100 GMT).
It will bring together researchers, youth and sports associations, trade unions, outdoor and rural organisations, religious communities, and rights groups.
"Never before have so many organisations taken part in a Swedish climate demonstration," Rindevall said. "The commitment is massive."
According to a Verian opinion poll published by public broadcaster SVT on Thursday, 37 percent of respondents said the climate was their top priority in the election, behind only health care, education, crime and elderly care.
The government has argued that the phase-out of fossil fuels must be gradual in order to preserve and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness and its companies.

items.title: Swedish police identify 17-year-old girl as victim in school sword attack
items.summary: Swedish police revealed that a 17-year-old student was the fatal victim of a sword attack at a high school where widespread tributes were paid to her Saturday.
items.body_text:
Flowers and candles were left outside the Brinell school in Fagersta where Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson went on Saturday morning to honour the dead student and three wounded victims.
The 18-year-old attacker entered the school on Friday afternoon -- just days after the school in the town of 13,000 people had returned from its summer break. He has since been detained by police.
"The person killed in this incident is a young 17-year-old female. Her family has been informed," police said on their website without giving any other identity details.
Minnea, a Brinell student who also went to honour the victims on Saturday, told the SVT broadcaster: "It's terrible to think that someone you sat at the same table with, someone you talked to, is suddenly dead."
Local authorities said that two boys aged 12 and 17 were seriously wounded in the attack, with one of them requiring emergency surgery. The third sustained light injuries.
READ ALSO: UPDATE: One dead, three wounded after sword attack at Swedish high school
Motive unknown
Local police chief Tommy Alriksson told reporters on Friday that investigators were seeking a motive for the latest violence to shock Sweden.
"We are looking into several leads... We are trying, of course, to remain as open-minded as possible," Alriksson said.
But few details have emerged about the attacker.
SVT reported that the perpetrator had a previous assault conviction and wore a helmet and carried a sword -- reminiscent of a 2015 school attack in the western town of Trollhattan in which a 21-year-old killed three people in a racially motivated attack.
Media reported a TikTok account belonging to the youth was being investigated. The account has been taken down.
AFP viewed the account before it was taken down and it had several videos referencing school attacks. The last update showed a photo of a sword.
"The police investigation is proceeding at full speed," police added in their statement on Saturday.
So far, officers have conducted around 80 interviews and are planning to question nearly all the school's staff and students -- amounting to almost 450 people, according to police chief Alriksson. Two addresses linked to the attacker in Fagersta were also searched.
Nellie Strandberg, a 16-year-old Brinell student, said she was on her way to the school's library when the assailant entered the institution.
"We were just going to collect some things and get ready for Monday. Then I see I guy who's bloody all down his back," she told the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.
Sweden has suffered other attacks at educational institutions. In February 2025, a 35-year-old man killed 10 people at an adult education centre in Orebro. In March 2022, an 18-year-old student stabbed two teachers to death at a secondary school in the southern city of Malmo.

items.title: What you need to know if you're getting divorced in Sweden
items.summary: Whether you moved to Sweden for love or relocated with a partner, sometimes a marriage just doesn't work out. Understanding how to navigate the administrative side can at least make it more straightforward.
items.body_text:
Divorce is simplest in an administrative sense if both partners are agreed about ending the marriage and neither of them has custody of a child aged under 16. In this case, they can apply for a divorce immediately, and the request usually takes only a few weeks to process. This is also possible even if the partners share custody if they have already lived apart for at least two years.
If these criteria are not met, including if one partner does not wish to get divorced, or if they have children (and have not lived apart for two years), there's an extra step to the process.
In these cases, the couple must enter a six-month period of reflection, and if they are still committed to the divorce at the end of that, they must file a second application. If both spouses want to, they can also request this period of reflection even if their situation doesn't require it.
Unlike many countries, there's no need to provide a reason for choosing to dissolve the marriage; it's enough to submit both partners' personal details.
It's also useful to know that you are always entitled to a translator when contacting Swedish government authorities and courts, including district courts and the Tax Agency, for example.
READERS' INSIGHTS:
How do I get divorced?
To start the process, you'll need to contact the district court (tingsrätt in Swedish) in the county where you're registered. You can find out which one that is here.
Then, you fill out a "joint application for divorce" form, or this form if only one partner wants to initiate a divorce.
You'll need to include a personbevis for both partners, which can be obtained from the Swedish Tax Agency (Skatteverket) here.
If you need to go through the six-month reconsideration period, the process is similar. In this instance, you'll receive a message from the district court after you submit your application, which will give you a case number and will state when your reflection period begins.
After six months have passed, you must resubmit an application, including re-sending your personbevis, to confirm you still want the divorce. There's no dedicated form for this, so it's sufficient to write on a normal piece of paper that you want to proceed with the divorce, and cite the case number.
It's not necessary for both partners to be in agreement about filing for divorce in order for it to be processed, but if neither partner proceeds with the application within six months of the reflection period ending (in other words, within a year of the start of the reflection period), the case is dismissed and the partners remain married.

How does division of property work?
Usually, all so-called matrimonial property will be divided equally between both divorcing partners. This includes property, cars, money in bank accounts and other items which were bought for both partners to share.
This is the case no matter how much each partner paid towards the property or what proportion each partner owns. If one partner will keep the property, the default is that they must then pay the other partner 50 percent of the market value (not the original price).
Each partner is considered to be responsible for their own financial situation after a divorce, but in certain circumstances it's possible to apply for financial support from the other partner during a transition period (see the relevant law, in Swedish, here). This depends on both the need for support and the other partner's ability to provide it. In some situations, this can be extended for a longer period of time.
In complex cases, particularly if the split is acrimonious and/or if one partner has given up a lot during the marriage (such as moving overseas or needing to give up work), it may be advisable to find a family lawyer.
