items.title: China mulls bid to host 2028 UN climate talks: sources
items.summary: China is mulling a bid to host UN climate talks in 2028, two sources familiar with the matter told AFP Friday, as it seeks to burnish its reputation as a leader in the fight against global warming. Beijing has not yet made a final decision regarding the proposal for the COP33 summit, both sources said, nor […]
items.body_text:
China is mulling a bid to host UN climate talks in 2028, two sources familiar with the matter told AFP Friday, as it seeks to burnish its reputation as a leader in the fight against global warming.
Beijing has not yet made a final decision regarding the proposal for the COP33 summit, both sources said, nor is there a clear timeline for doing so. The host does not have to be decided this year.
China’s interest was first reported by Bloomberg News.
The UN’s annual climate gatherings rotate among regional blocs. This year’s COP31 is scheduled to take place in Turkey, followed by COP32 in Ethiopia in 2027.
The 2028 summit falls to the Asia-Pacific.
In April, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 without specifying a reason. South Korea has previously expressed interest.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a query for comment.
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) secretariat told AFP: “We have not been informed by the Asia-Pacific Regional Group on the nomination of the host country for COP33.
“Regional groups hold consultations first to determine which country from their respective regions will offer to host on behalf of the group. Once agreed, the chair of that regional group formally sends an official nomination to the secretariat.”
China has in recent years positioned itself as a counterweight to the United States.
Under President Donald Trump, the US left the landmark Paris climate agreement twice while the administration seeks to boost fossil fuels.
Hosting UN climate talks could thus be an opportunity for China to boost its credentials as a climate leader.
The world’s second-largest economy also has an economic interest as the leading exporter of green technologies, including solar panels, electric vehicles, wind turbines and batteries.
US-China dynamics
But hosting the gathering could also cast an unwelcome spotlight on China, which, with its population of 1.4 billion and massive manufacturing industry, is the world’s biggest greenhouse emitter, followed by the United States, India and the European Union.
Although it has pledged to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060, it is targeting only a modest 7-10 percent reduction in economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, compared to peak levels.
Another piece that China is considering is the US-China dynamic, one source said.
Climate cooperation had been a key feature of the bilateral relationship under former presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, and COP33 could spur renewed collaboration if a Democrat is elected in 2028.
The summit would likely fall days after the US presidential election to replace Trump.
“The dynamics between the US and China have been a force for both progress and tension over the 35-year history of the climate regime, and the larger US-China relationship will continue to be challenging regardless of the outcome of the next election,” Alden Meyer of the climate change think tank E3G told AFP.

items.title: ‘So bad it’s good’: Rough animated film Niu Lai becomes surprise Chinese hit
items.summary: A low-budget Chinese animated film that was widely mocked for its crude visuals became a viral hit, with people packing cinemas to see just how bad it is. “Niu Lai”, which translates to “Here Comes the Cow”, earned around 7,000 yuan ($1,000) in its opening week from August 5, before surging to 33.06 million yuan […]
items.body_text:
A low-budget Chinese animated film that was widely mocked for its crude visuals became a viral hit, with people packing cinemas to see just how bad it is.
“Niu Lai”, which translates to “Here Comes the Cow”, earned around 7,000 yuan ($1,000) in its opening week from August 5, before surging to 33.06 million yuan ($4.92 million) at the Chinese box office, according to ticketing platform Maoyan.
The film, made by a mother and son, follows the journey of a calf named Niu Lai and was crafted frame by frame over five years, local media reported, with the duo also composing original scores for the end credits.
Caelan Moriarty, an American musician working in China, told AFP the film is “so bad that it’s so good”.
“I appreciate how bad it is, but there’s some heart (put) into it, so you can’t hate that,” the 25-year-old said.
Artificial intelligence could make the movie in “like ten seconds or even faster”, Moriarty said, but “the fact that they didn’t use AI, they took time” was impressive.
“It’s not perfect. But because it’s not perfect, it’s good, it shows how human it is… and I think that’s why this is trending.”
With its stiff 3D characters and awkward dialogue, the movie traces Niu Lai’s relationship with his mother. The film’s unpolished style quickly went viral on social media, with fans embracing its imperfections as part of its charm.
Student Stella Xing, who watched the film in Beijing after seeing memes online, told AFP: “Even though it’s pretty rough around the edges, there are so many funny details — like the way (Niu Lai) walks, for instance”.
“It’s hilarious and really makes people want to come see it,” she added.
‘Part of its appeal’
At cinemas in Beijing, hand-drawn banners of human-like cows with eyebrows stood in stark contrast to the glossy posters promoting Christopher Nolan’s latest film “The Odyssey”.
Barely any conventional marketing had been done to promote the film.
As “Niu Lai” took China’s internet by storm, online retailers on platforms such as Taobao rushed to produce merchandise featuring the yellow cow, including T-shirts, figurines and even boxer shorts.
One online merchant told AFP he started selling “Niu Lai” keychains as the movie became a hit.
The film offers “something different from the polished, sophisticated productions we are used to”, Pan Wang, an associate professor at Australia’s University of New South Wales, said.
“It is a bit like eating refined grains every day and then suddenly having some coarse grains for a change — the contrast itself feels refreshing,” Wang added.
“Its roughness, absurdity and imperfection become part of its appeal.”
Animated films have proven highly popular in the world’s second largest economy.
The more polished Chinese blockbuster “Ne Zha 2” ousted last year Disney’s “Inside Out 2” to become the highest-grossing animated film of all time.

The conviction of two pro-democracy figures who organised Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigils has prompted wide approval from government officials. Activists and overseas human rights groups, however, have expressed concern about what they see as declining freedoms in the city.
Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan, both former leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were found guilty on Friday of inciting subversion.
A third defendant, former lawmaker Albert Ho, pleaded guilty when the trial opened in January. The group itself – which organised mass vigils to remember those killed in China’s 1989 Tiananmen crackdown – was also found guilty.
Lee and Chow have already been on remand for nearly five years following their September 2021 arrests. Ho has been behind bars since May 2021 aside from a seven-month period of bail.
HKFP rounds up reactions to the convictions, which could see defendants jailed for up to 10 years.
Local reactions:
Hong Kong leader John Lee
“The Alliance had long been deliberately planting seeds of hatred against the CPC and the Central Government in the Hong Kong society, attempting to incite disaffection, hatred and other sentiments among members of the public against the CPC and the Central Government through various means, and inciting people to subvert state power. The acts of the defendants over a long period of time endangered national security; their conspiracy was abundantly clear, which must be brought to justice.”
Chief Superintendent Steve Li of the police’s National Security Department
“It is an indisputable fact that the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China has, year after year over a prolonged period, sown countless seeds of hatred against the Central Government and the Chinese Communist Party among the public. Today, the court’s conviction of the Alliance’s chairman and vice-chairmen rightly exposes their true colours as having deliberately incited others to subvert state power and endanger national security.”
Secretary for Security Chris Tang
“Since The Alliance’s founding, it has promoted its agenda with the aim of overthrowing the Chinese Communist Party’s leadership and constitution… after the national security law was enacted, the defendants still held public activities, including attempting to hold illegal assemblies, using slogans to incite the public to take part in so-called protests, distributing printed publications or online content, accepting media interviews, and making public statements. They also attempted to operate and digitise their so-called museum.”
Activists’ and family members’ reactions:
Elizabeth Tang, labour rights activist and Lee Cheuk-yan’s wife
“[I am] very angry, very disappointed. There’s been no evidence all along that there were illegal means, and yet [they are] still found guilty. It’s very disappointing, and I’m really angry. [I’ll] take a look at how to handle mitigation, or we may not [submit any mitigation materials].”
Emily Lau, former Democratic Party chair
“[The June 4 vigil] was held for so many years, and there were no issues right? And the government gave permission back then to use the venue too. A lot of us just really don’t understand it.”
Tsang Kin-shing, also known as “The Bull”
“Regarding the verdict today, I feel helpless. In the future, if you ask whether we should take part in candlelight vigils, I would warn everyone not to because it’s easy to break the law. The tears of the candlelight will flow in our hearts.”
Lau Ka-yee, former executive committee member of the Alliance
“To prove that June Fourth and commemorating it is not a crime, we will continue this legal path and lay bare the truth as we know it. This will allow the public to see clearly what the arguments actually are. Justice resides in the hearts of the people.”

items.body_text:
Major tech firms to help upskill Hong Kong workers under ‘AI for All’: Paul Chan
Finance chief warns frontier tech will challenge the job market, urging faster action to equip young people with AI skills and workplace opportunities
Hong Kong’s employees retraining board will partner with major tech firms to launch an artificial intelligence (AI) training programme for the working population in November, the city’s finance chief has said.
In his Sunday blog, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the HK$50 million (US$6.4 million) “AI for All” inclusive programme, announced in the February budget, would feature more than 200 activities and was expected to benefit 50,000 people within two years.
“The development and application of frontier technology will pose challenges to the job market. We must speed up our response, helping young people master the skills and giving them opportunities to apply them in the workplace,” he said.
“Hong Kong is home to many small and medium-sized enterprises whose agility, adaptability, and innovative spirit have seen them through past tech shifts and economic cycles. As we navigate this current paradigm shift, we will fully support them in adapting, preparing, and continuing to grow.”
Chan cited a survey finding that almost 70 per cent of Hong Kong residents were proficient in using AI, while about 20 per cent were highly proficient and leveraged AI agents to automate daily tasks.
He said the report further estimated that if Hong Kong’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) could catch up to large corporations in AI adoption by 2035, it could unlock up to HK$65 billion in economic value for the city.

items.body_text:
Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
The plan is likely to prompt Tehran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf in a bid to push up oil prices and force Trump to retreat
President Donald Trump is betting new sanctions, a naval blockade and ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can accomplish what thousands of bombs and missiles could not: force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war on US terms.
But like other US efforts to force Iran into capitulation, there is one main problem: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has claimed control of the vital Strait of Hormuz and sent volleys of attack drones across the Gulf, may be impervious to such pressure – and has plenty of ways to retaliate.
A major part of the US effort will come on Monday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to unveil details of a plan designed to shift the conflict from tit-for-tat strikes across the Middle East to full-blown economic isolation – a campaign that could touch nations ranging from China and India to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
Yet significant new economic pressure is likely to prompt Iran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf, including against energy infrastructure, in an attempt to push up oil prices and raise the cost of the US effort, forcing Trump to shift his approach once again.
“If this is actually effective, at some point, Iran will lash out again – they just will have no alternative,” said Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who worked on Iran issues at the State Department and White House National Security Council until last year. “Trump may see this as a different phase of the war, but I don’t think Iran does.”
Since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has repeatedly shown the ability to endure air strikes on thousands of targets, layers of sanctions and a US navy blockade – yet still retain the ability to hit back.
items.normalised_title: why trumps economic pain could spark more iranian attacks on gulf nations

items.body_text:
South Koreans ‘intoxicated by stocks’ swarmed market frenzy – and lost everything
‘I don’t think I will ever invest in the Kospi again,’ says an emotionally drained retiree who, like others, is reeling from the rout
It has also raised questions about how South Korea, a tech powerhouse, can progress to developed market status when it hosts such extreme behaviour by retail investors, known locally as “ants” for their tendency to swarm into trades.
“Ultimately many who entered the market may have suffered severe losses and a majority of them could become so traumatised that they lose interest in investing altogether,” said Jeon Suk-jae, a YouTuber whose investment channel has 3.7 million subscribers.
In the two months since the market’s peak, Jeon has seen the comments on his channel, which hosts videos like the one titled “the entire nation is intoxicated by stocks”, flip from euphoria to gloom, broadly tracking the national mood.
Beyond the losses – some realised, some still on paper – there is a psychological reckoning that the nation’s leaders are dealing with.
Demand for psychiatric help is rising and other signs of stress are rattling the public. Police in Busan said they had arrested a man in his 20s who is suspected of attempted murder over the stabbing of a YouTuber he allegedly blamed for his stock losses.

items.body_text:
花蓮山區恐有豪雨 萬里溪堰塞湖發布黃色警戒
花蓮萬里溪堰塞湖23日上午6時40分空拍畫面。（林保署花蓮分署提供）
受到強西南風、低壓帶影響，中央氣象署預報，嘉義以南、東半部地區慎防大雨或豪雨，尤其南部地區，今晚起花蓮山區慎防豪雨等級以上降雨。農業部林業及自然保育署花蓮分署今指出，依據中央氣象署今天下午2點發布未來24小時定量降水預報（QPF）281.7mm，已達發布黃色警戒標準。
林保署花蓮分署今下午3點指出，因應0822低壓帶及西南風豪雨，依據中央氣象署今天下午2點發布未來24小時定量降水預報（QPF）281.7mm，依據「花蓮萬里溪堰塞湖溢流後警戒機制表」，發布黃色警戒，惟河道範圍內維持紅色警戒管制；請地方政府（花蓮縣政府、鳳林鎮公所、萬榮鄉公所）通知影響範圍內住戶注意避難外，另請相關單位提前執行預防性防災措施。
林保署花蓮分署指出，萬里溪堰塞湖今天（23日）下午2點10分，水位高程為1092.16m、蓄水量634.22萬立方公尺。黃色警戒對象與範圍包含萬榮鄉萬榮村、明利村，鳳林鎮森榮里、長橋里、山興里、鳳信里、大榮里、北林里等聚落，以及台鐵、公路台9線萬里溪橋、西寶大橋，請地方政府落實西寶及箭瑛2座橋梁管制作業，另加強河道巡視。
紅色警戒對象與範圍為萬里溪河道，以及農田水利取水設施、台灣自來水公司萬榮淨水場設施以及水利河防構造物等公共設施，林保署花蓮分署指出，下游河道仍處於紅色警戒狀態，為慎重計，請農田水利署、鳳林鎮公所，關閉灌溉水門。萬里溪下游河川區域範圍內各施工單位，並請通知相關施工廠商；台電公司所屬的鳳林超高壓變電所，雖非位於警戒範圍，但須注意保護措施。
依據「花蓮萬里溪堰塞湖溢流後警戒機制表」，若未來24小時預測累積雨量大於200mm，將發布黃色警戒，針對保全戶中有獨居長者、臥病、行動不便等，請地方政府執行預警性撤離，提前將弱勢族群（行動不便或需旁人攙扶者）等先行撤離，並完成避難收容所開設前的空間物資人員整備；若未來12小時預測累積雨量大於200mm，將發布紅色警戒，保全戶就需要強制性疏散撤離。
「花蓮萬里溪堰塞湖溢流後警戒機制表」，未來24小時預測累積雨量大於200mm發布黃色警戒。（林保署花蓮分署提供）

高雄大雨下不停 國1楠梓段轎車打滑連撞
轎車疑因天雨路滑操作不當，先撞擊護欄，再碰撞內側車道另一部轎車，肇事車主輕傷自行就醫。（國道警提供）
高雄市今（23）日豪大雨不斷，1部轎車中午行經國道1號北向357.7公里（楠梓路段），疑因天雨路滑操作不當，撞擊護欄並碰撞內側車道轎車，肇事車主輕傷自行就醫。
國道警察5隊初步調查，事故發生在中午12點47分，26歲轎車駕駛吳男當時行經國1北向357.7公里外側車道，疑因天雨路滑操作不當，先撞擊內側護欄後，再與內側車道的王男車子發生碰撞，吳男受輕傷自行就醫。
各車駕駛人酒測值均為0，現場於下午1點17分排除，全線恢復通車，真正肇事原因及肇責尚待警方進一步釐清。

items.body_text:
黃世杰談龍潭發展 位處台積電、無人機等科技產業發展關鍵位置
民進黨桃園市長參選人黃世杰（左）出席桃園市議員參選人張贊聞（右）舉辦的「心桃園政見說明會」。（記者李容萍攝）
民進黨桃園市長參選人黃世杰今（23）日再度走訪龍潭，出席桃園市議員參選人張贊聞舉辦的「心桃園政見說明會」。黃世杰表示，龍潭不只是桃園重要的客家文化重鎮，更位處台積電、無人機等科技產業發展關鍵位置，未來若由他擔任市長，將積極與地方溝通、整合中央資源，向全國及國際招商，讓產業扎根桃園、人才留在家鄉，打造桃園成為台灣走向世界的重要城市。
包括衛福部次長呂建德、民進黨桃園市黨部主委張火爐等人到場力挺。
黃世杰表示，走進龍潭能感受到深厚文化底蘊與地方持續向前的生命力，龍潭正站在下一階段城市發展的重要轉折點。尤其台積電有望重新回到龍科三期，更讓地方燃起期待。他說，過去3年不少龍潭人、桃園人都對台積電進駐一度生變感到惋惜，如今在中央及竹科管理局積極努力下，機會重新出現，桃園更應珍惜並全力把握。
黃世杰指出，城市發展難免伴隨不同意見，尤其土地徵收及產業開發涉及許多家庭與地方生活，更需要政府勇於承擔責任。市府不能只是推動開發，更應主動走進地方，與居民、民意代表及產業界充分溝通，說明產業轉型能帶來的改變，並提出交通、生活、就業、環境及產業的完整規劃，讓建設真正回應市民期待。
他強調，未來若擔任市長，將與中央、竹科管理局及台積電攜手合作，除爭取重大企業落腳，也將吸引上下游產業鏈進駐，讓桃園不只是工廠所在地，更成為工作、生活與成家都能兼顧的城市。他希望桃園年輕人未來不必為了好工作每天往返台北、新竹，而能在家鄉找到舞台、實現理想，讓產業發展成果真正留在桃園。
黃世杰提到，龍潭原本就是台灣無人機產業重要聚落，面對全球科技競爭及民主供應鏈重組，桃園應把握機會，從產業聚落、人才培育到國際合作全面布局，成為台灣重要科技城市及與國際民主夥伴交流的窗口。
黃世杰大力推薦張贊聞，認為張長期站在第一線，熟悉地方人事物，以真誠態度傾聽鄉親心聲，已做好進入市議會準備，盼鄉親給優秀在地子弟機會，成為龍潭的聲音，與新市府並肩打拚，讓文化被看見、產業有未來、年輕人願意留下來，共同打造更有希望的龍潭。

items.title: North Korea military officer discharged over wife’s Chinese relative
items.summary: North Korean authorities recently discharged a military officer stationed in Hamhung after discovering that his wife has a relative in China who is an ethnic Korean-Chinese. The abrupt dismissal has fueled suspicion inside his unit that a power struggle over his position, not the relative, was the real motive. A source in South Hamgyong province […]
items.body_text:
North Korean authorities recently discharged a military officer stationed in Hamhung after discovering that his wife has a relative in China who is an ethnic Korean-Chinese. The abrupt dismissal has fueled suspicion inside his unit that a power struggle over his position, not the relative, was the real motive.
A source in South Hamgyong province told Daily NK on Thursday that the officer served in the rear services department of a division under the army’s Seventh Corps, a regional army command and only learned of his wife’s Chinese relative when his commanders informed him of the discharge.
When the officer married, background investigators screened his wife and her immediate family without flagging any issues. The relative’s status in China went unmentioned throughout his subsequent years of service.
The officer reached his rank through an unusual path within North Korea’s military. He enlisted as an ordinary soldier and served as a clerk in the rear services department and later became an officer without attending a military academy. That route is known informally in North Korea’s military as a jikbal, or direct promotion. Such promotions typically trigger a thorough background check of the candidate and his family.
Even so, background checks for officers outside the political and security departments tend to be narrower, the source said. Investigators closely scrutinize a spouse and immediate family, but they rarely trace distant relatives. That gap is why the Chinese relative went unnoticed for years.
The belated discovery struck colleagues and the officer himself as suspicious. The same relative, after all, had raised no concern at his wedding or during his years of service. “People here find it hard to believe he was discharged now over a background issue that never came up before,” the source said. “Some have said someone else may have needed his position.”
Rivalry may explain North Korea military officer’s discharge
Rear services officers tend to draw envy from colleagues in other departments, the source said. The rear services department manages a unit’s food, clothing and other supplies. That role leaves its officers widely seen as enjoying more comfortable living conditions than their peers.
“Officers in the political department and the security department have always viewed rear services officers with some resentment because they live so well,” the source said. The political department oversees ideological education within the unit, while the security department monitors loyalty and internal threats. “Because of that, families of rear services officers are careful even about how they dress, so as not to draw attention from other officers’ families,” the source added.
The officer’s background may have made him a bigger target for envy than most. It is unusual for an officer promoted directly from the ranks to reach a division-level rear services post, and most officers in such positions trained at a military academy instead, the source said.
“Reaching the division level as a jikbal officer usually requires some backing,” the source said. “There’s a growing view that a power struggle between officers played a role in his discharge.”
It remains unconfirmed whether internal rivalries among officers, or tensions between their families, directly influenced the discharge, the source said.

items.title: In North Korea, homes near markets fetch triple pre-pandemic prices
items.summary: Housing prices near a market in the North Korean city of Chongjin have climbed as much as three times their pre-pandemic levels in 2026. Homes closest to the market are commanding the steepest premiums, a source in North Hamgyong province told Daily NK. Prices around Sunam Market, one of Chongjin’s largest, have risen sharply since […]
items.body_text:
Housing prices near a market in the North Korean city of Chongjin have climbed as much as three times their pre-pandemic levels in 2026. Homes closest to the market are commanding the steepest premiums, a source in North Hamgyong province told Daily NK.
Prices around Sunam Market, one of Chongjin’s largest, have risen sharply since before the COVID-19 pandemic. A home’s size and condition now matter less than how close it sits to the market, and locals sometimes call the added value a jangmadang premium, using a Korean term for informal markets. Such markets emerged after North Korea’s centrally planned economy unraveled in the 1990s.
A rundown, one-room house resembling a storage shed sold for 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese yuan before the pandemic, or about $1,500 to $2,200. The same type of house now trades for roughly 30,000 yuan, two to three times its former price.
A one-room house with basic amenities has followed a similar path. It rose from 20,000 to 25,000 yuan before the pandemic to about 50,000 yuan today. A standard two-room house has climbed even further, from 40,000 to 50,000 yuan to roughly 100,000 yuan over the same period.
Two-room houses close enough to Sunam Market to double as a shop or storage space have posted the sharpest gains. Such homes sold for 50,000 to 60,000 yuan before the pandemic. They now fetch as much as 150,000 yuan, nearly triple their earlier value.
“Around Sunam Market, demand from people looking to secure business space outweighs demand from those simply looking for a place to live,” the source said. “Even for two-room houses of the same size, the price is far higher if the house is close to the market.”
Market access, not size, drives housing prices
Houses near Sunam Market carry a heavy premium because they can double as warehouses or private shops, not just as homes, the source explained. Closeness to the market and usefulness for business have become bigger price drivers than size or condition, and the shift underscores how deeply market forces have reshaped housing in North Korea’s provincial cities.
Brokers have increasingly taken over the paperwork involved in these sales, which includes transferring the name on a residence-use permit, the document that authorizes a household to occupy state-owned housing. In the past, buyers paid bribes directly to the housing department of the local people’s committee to handle the process themselves. Brokers now manage both the sale and the required government filings, the source said.
The shift coincides with a local development push that has driven construction of 12-story or taller apartments in provincial cities. Developers once delivered new housing with only the frame and exterior plaster finished, leaving buyers to complete interior work themselves. Increasingly, they hand over units with finished interiors and furniture already installed.
Prices in the new high-rises vary sharply by floor, the source said. In one high-rise in Hyesan, Ryanggang province, units on the first through sixth floors sell for about 30,000 yuan. Those on the seventh through ninth floors go for roughly 25,000 yuan. Units above the 10th floor sell for even less, the source said.
Higher floors tend to be cheaper for a simple reason. Chronic electricity shortages often leave elevators out of service, forcing residents to climb the stairs. That adds to the daily strain of life in the buildings.
The pattern reflects how thoroughly market forces have taken hold across North Korea’s provincial cities. A house’s proximity to markets and its potential for commercial use now shape its price more than size or condition. The practical convenience of daily life factors in as well, the source said.

items.title: North Korea weather agency faces month-long ideological review
items.summary: North Korea’s State Hydro-Meteorological Administration is undergoing a sweeping, party-ordered ideological review this month after a string of forecasting failures worsened storm and heat wave damage across the country in 2026. The ruling Workers’ Party of Korea has ordered agency staff and workers at related institutions to hold monthlong self-criticism sessions starting in mid-August. A […]
items.body_text:
North Korea’s State Hydro-Meteorological Administration is undergoing a sweeping, party-ordered ideological review this month after a string of forecasting failures worsened storm and heat wave damage across the country in 2026. The ruling Workers’ Party of Korea has ordered agency staff and workers at related institutions to hold monthlong self-criticism sessions starting in mid-August.
A source told Daily NK on Thursday that the Central Committee of the Workers’ Party of Korea recently held the State Hydro-Meteorological Administration responsible for a series of forecasting failures. The committee ordered agency departments and cells to hold general assemblies for one month and to produce strongly worded self-criticism statements, according to the source.
The order, issued Aug. 8, applies not only to the State Hydro-Meteorological Administration but to all related institutions nationwide, including local weather observation stations, the source said.
The committee sharply rebuked the agency for failing to accurately forecast the abnormal weather that persisted from June through early August, saying the failure worsened damage across the country, according to the source.
This year’s monsoon season ran unusually long, and the country was hit by a record heat wave. The agency failed to properly predict the timing of localized heavy rain and sudden temperature spikes, leaving the country unprepared for the resulting damage to farmland and infrastructure, the source said.
Party blames ideology, not aging equipment
The committee also focused criticism on the agency’s failure to carry out a core party directive to overhaul the country’s early warning system. It sharply criticized delays in reporting and lapses in scientific analysis as well, the source said.
“Behind the party’s sweeping ideological review targeting the entire weather-related establishment is an intent to blame the damage from the forecasting failures on workers’ ideological laxity and negligence in carrying out party policy, rather than on technical or environmental limitations,” the source said.
Agency workers and technicians are currently struggling to focus on their regular duties because of the harsh, monthlong ideological review, and they are anxiously watching how the process unfolds, the source said.
The Central Committee is requiring workers to dig through the past three months of their work for errors and submit harsh self-criticism statements. Depending on the outcome of the review, some workers could face personnel penalties or even “revolutionization,” a punitive measure in North Korea that typically involves reassignment to hard labor. That possibility has added to the sense of unease inside the agency.
Some State Hydro-Meteorological Administration workers have complained privately that the review ignores deeper problems, the source said.
“Underlying problems like aging observation equipment and a shortage of satellite data are being left untouched, while forecast errors are being blamed on ideology. That only breeds resentment and a sense of futility,” the source said, describing the workers’ complaints.
Other workers voiced exhaustion at having to write self-criticism statements and criticize each other for hours each day throughout the assembly period, the source said.
“If we spend all day writing self-criticism statements and tearing each other down in general assemblies for an entire month, how are we supposed to handle the critical overnight weather monitoring duties of summer?” the source said, relaying workers’ concerns.

items.title: Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
items.summary: Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match. Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
items.body_text:
Australia vs Bangladesh quick hits: Shoriful Islam's ball of the series, more Mitchell Starc carnage in the 29th two-day Test
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.
Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
1. Shoriful's ball of the series
It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.
The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.
With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.
And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.
The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.
The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.
And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …
2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage
Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.
Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.
And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.
He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.
And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.
An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.
Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.
3. Smith takes a screamer after tea
Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.
Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.
And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.
He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.
Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.
4. The shortest session ever?
With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.
However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.
He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.
But it was all over with the very next ball.
Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.
With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.
5. The 29th two-day Test

As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.

Sydney Swans AFLW captain says support 'just unbelievable' as crowd record smashed in emotional week
Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy wasn't sure what to expect for her side when they ran out for the first instalment of a historic double-header at the SCG.
The Swans dominated headlines across the country all week, filling both front and back pages of every newspaper, for a scandal that called the club's culture into question.
What the women's team got was an outpouring of support which broke the side's attendance record with 16,672 fans filling the stands to watch them play.
That is more than double the previous club record of 8,264.
"It's amazing. We weren't sure what we were going to expect this week, but to see the support that we've received today is just unbelievable," McEvoy told Fox Footy after the game.
"The members and fans are so tight and they know that we're united as a club and we're better than what we were at the start of the week.
"I'm just so grateful to have the support that we had today and the girls were able to turn it on.
"We had a few nervous girls, that's for sure, but we absolutely turned it on."
The scenes were particularly celebratory on the ground post-siren, after Sydney beat Essendon by 24 points.
It was just the second time the women have played on the SCG for premiership points and the first in a double billing with the men's.
Before locking in to warm up, star men's players Errol Gulden and captain Callum Mills got around the women's players.
Gulden was also seen going up to the crowd giving the fans a big thank you for turning out in droves.
Some of those fans left before the men's game, as a boycott had been suggested in the days before the match as a scandal continues to engulf the club.
It's unclear how many fans left in protest to the scandal, but a steady stream was seen leaving.
Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.
Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.
Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.
Lulu Clarke, who has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, was one of the fans who walked out.
Ms Clarke had bought a ticket to the men's game, unaware the women were also playing, but once the news broke of the incident she knew she would not be staying for both games.
"Of late, I've definitely drifted apart from the Swans and the AFL industry as a whole," Ms Clarke said.
"I decided that I'm absolutely not going to the men's game, even if those five players were still stood down. There's no way I could just show up and watch it. It just didn't sit right with me."
Former Matilda Sarah Walsh also left the stadium after the women's game, saying it had been a "tough week", but stressed she was not boycotting the men's team.
"It's not a new story but I have a five-year-old daughter who I brought here today to support the women's team," Ms Walsh said.
"I think you can have a club and not expect someone to be a fan of both teams.
"I think that's the nuance of sport, don't expect Socceroos fans to be Matildas fans … We've got a long way to go in society. I don't think this is a Sydney Swans issue at all … it's a societal issue and we all need to do better."
Swans fans Kayley and Georgia told ABC News they were there to support the women and will likely just watch a bit of the men's game.
"It's very disappointing from the men's team … I feel like we were very disappointed in everything that happened," Georgia said.
Kayley said the situation was upsetting.
"We've been supporting the Swans since we were kids as well. So, it was just shocking," she said.

items.title: Cummins refuses to confirm Labuschagne’s fate as Starc inspires two-day win
items.summary: Mitchell Starc’s heroics with the ball have again papered over the cracks in Australia’s batting line-up. But with a big tour on the horizon, it might not be enough to save Marnus Labuschagne.
items.body_text:
Cummins refuses to confirm Labuschagne’s fate as Starc inspires two-day win
Updated ,first published
Mackay: Australian skipper Pat Cummins would not confirm if Marnus Labuschagne would board the plane for October’s three-Test series in South Africa, after the under-siege Queenslander endured another poor outing in his side’s emphatic triumph over Bangladesh in the second Test.
While Cummins’ men cruised to victory by an innings and 51 runs inside two days, Labuschagne’s woes with the bat continued on day one, falling for just four runs, victim to a ball which brushed his thigh pad and fell onto leg stump. The 32-year-old’s most recent century at Test level dates back to July 2023, and he has averaged just 29.69 since the start of that year.
“I don’t reckon I can guarantee anyone really, he [Labuschagne] has not scored the runs he would’ve liked,” Cummins said.
“I did say a couple of days ago – and I think it still stands – he’s been batting fantastically well off the field. But it doesn’t mean much – you’ve got to convert that into runs out there.
“We’ve got a bit of time. [The] selectors will get together, I’m sure, in the next week or two, and start nutting out that next Test squad. We know he’s class when he’s at his best. And going into this series, we thought he was pretty close to his best.
“But he needs to start transferring that into runs out there, so we’ll see in the next couple of weeks.”
Labuschagne was not alone in failing as Australia only managed to amass 210. But the dominance of their bowlers meant they did not require a second innings to register the quickfire win, bowling out the visitors for 64 and 95.
It meant the first Test played in Mackay ended inside two days, just like last November’s Perth Ashes Test and the Boxing Day Test a month later at the MCG.
In fact, Australia’s 210 was lowest recorded by any team that has won a Test by an innings in the past 80 years – and the fourth lowest to do so of all time. The Test was the second-shortest completed on Australian soil, lasting just 750 deliveries, compared to the 656-ball Test against South Africa at the MCG in 1932.
Mitchell Starc was the inspiration for Australia’s stark turnaround following the nine-wicket loss in the first Test in Darwin a week earlier.

items.body_text:
A radical overhaul of Victoria’s highest court, proposed by the Liberal party to increase sentences, has been criticised by legal and human rights groups who warn it would politicise the judiciary.
The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Sunday announced that if elected in November the Coalition would split the court of appeal in two, creating a dedicated court of criminal appeal alongside a separate court of civil appeal.
It would appoint additional judges with expertise in criminal law to the new court of criminal appeal.
The overhaul would be introduced alongside tougher bail and sentencing laws, which the Coalition has committed to enacting before the end of the year if it wins government.
Together, the measures would help set new legal precedents which the Coalition said would ultimately lead to tougher sentences for serious offences.
“It’s time for a new approach,” Wilson said on Sunday. “Our new criminal court will empower specialist criminal law judges to ensure sentencing of criminals meet community expectations. Each sentence they hand down will form part of case law going forward, helping to establish appropriate consequences for criminal actions.
In Victoria, judges are appointed by the governor on the recommendation of the attorney general. The shadow attorney general, James Newbury, said “nothing will change” about that process, though a “strong background in criminal matters will be a key focus” when making appointments.
“[It] will mean that criminal matters are dealt with by specialist judges who will be tough on crime, who will be tough on criminal offences,” he said.
Newbury said he had “consulted in a way that Victorians would expect” with judges and the courts about the policy, though he said it would be inappropriate to discuss the consultation publicly.
Legal and human rights groups, however, have criticised the proposal.
Gemma Cafarella, the president of Liberty Victoria, described it as a “dangerous and ignorant thought bubble designed without the input of experts”.
She said in “properly functioning democracies” parliaments make the laws and courts apply them, with the two systems kept seperate.
“Governments shouldn’t choose judges to get the outcomes they want,” Cafarella said. “This is a move that would politicise the criminal courts, and it must be rejected.”
She said the comments by the Coalition were by implication an “appalling political attack on the work of court of appeal judges”.
The Australian Lawyers Alliance criminal justice spokesperson, Greg Barns SC, said there was “no clear evidence” the court of appeal structure was failing, “aside from the longstanding issue of underfunding”.
“This is a disturbing example of the risk of undermining the independence of the judiciary,” he said. “It sends a signal that the opposition is willing to interfere with judicial independence for political purposes.”
The Alliance’s director, Susan Accary, said they were “not persuaded” splitting the courts would improve the quality of justice or address delays in the system.
Tom Ballantyne, president of the Law Institute of Victoria, said it was unclear how the proposal “adds anything” to the court of appeal, as it “already has access to numerous judges with extensive criminal expertise”.
“Anything that could undermine the independence of the courts and its judges could have significant consequences and would be a significant concern to the community,” he said.
Earlier this month One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said the party wanted to make “bleeding heart judges accountable” and “get rid” of those he believes fail to meet community expectations.
Crime continues to be a major issue in the lead-up to the November election, with the Labor government having already passed controversial “adult time for violent crime” and tougher bail laws. It is also undertaking a review of sentencing.

items.body_text:
The One Nation MP David Farley says the minor party’s net migration target is “not too different” to Labor’s, forcing his leader to issue an urgent clarification amid rising confusion over the policy.
It is the second time Pauline Hanson has had to issue a correction after the member for Farrer seemed to contradict One Nation’s restrictive approach to immigration.
Appearing on the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday morning, Farley argued skilled workers and backpackers were critical to keeping Australia fed, and argued they should be considered as a separate category to migration “in its true form”.
The minor rightwing party, led by Hanson, has struggled to define its migration policy, with inconsistent messaging over whether its target figure represents net overseas migration (Nom) or permanent migration.
The member for Farrer said One Nation’s Nom target remained 130,000. But he said that figure did not include skilled workers, backpackers and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.
Farley said he expected there would be room for a “minimum” 100,000 additional people in the migration target to ensure critical industries had enough workers. Those included about 40,000 Palm workers and 70,000 skilled workers, including aged care nurses.
“A minimum of 100 [thousand additional migrant workers], but the 130,000 [target] is what we call the true Nom,” he told ABC’s Insiders on Sunday.
“I think the big difference is [that] we’re focusing on: what are the skills we need as a nation, where do we need these migrants to be.
“The raw number is not too different [to the government’s], but the reality is, where do we need them? We don’t need them in the great urban metroplex. We need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining.”
But Hanson issued an implied rebuke to her MP on Sunday afternoon, with a post on social media insisting “One Nation’s policy is to cut net overseas migration to 130,000”.
Hanson said: “Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration.”
In fact, seasonal workers who live in Australia for 12 months over a 16-month period are included in the Nom.
The Nom is calculated by the difference between the number of people entering and leaving the country who have lived in or out of the country for 12 months over a 16-month period. It includes Australians moving abroad and returning but excludes short-term visitors, such as tourists.
The Nom is different to permanent migration, which measures longer-term visas offered to skilled workers and family members. For this financial year, there are 185,000 permanent places.
The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said One Nation has “somehow managed to turn one headline number (130,000) into at least half a dozen different immigration policies”.
“One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy?” he said.
Energy minister, Chris Bowen, said: “I’m not sure what One Nation is saying about immigration because it appears to me, based on what Mr Farley said, that One Nation now agrees with the approach of the government. And obviously I’d welcome that.”
The Nom figure surged after the pandemic, during which it fell below zero, but has began to return to more typical levels in recent quarters.
The Nom was forecast to drop to 295,000 people last financial year but reached 301,000. The government forecasts it to drop further to 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 in 2027-28.
The Albanese government is preparing to announce changes to the migration system to achieve Nom targets.
The Coalition has declined to provide an exact figure for its Nom target, but the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has indicated it will be “well below 200,000”.

items.title: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
items.summary: A Palestinian-American has returned to his home in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra to protect it from Israeli settlers, amid a surge in attacks and settlement expansion.
items.body_text:
Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
"I can't go outside": Israeli settler attacks higher than any year on record, driving settlement expansion
The recent siege of Palestinian homes by militant Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank is far from an isolated incident.
But the U.S. citizenship of one of the Palestinian homeowners has drawn more media attention than the near-daily acts of aggression by hardline Jewish settlers aimed at pushing Palestinians from their land typically receive.
Ohio-based businessman Loui Ridi returned to Qusra on Monday, August 17, to protect his home – and his brother and nephew, who live there — as settlers encircled it and two nearby homes.
"I called my brother and he said, 'I have no food. I don't want to leave the house, but I need food,'" Ridi told CBC news in a video call from Qusra after his arrival.
For them to leave, he said, would be to invite the settlers to take his home.
"Just two months ago [settlers] were at my neighbour's village in Jalud," he said. "They put a siege on the family for a couple of weeks. And unfortunately, they managed to kick them out of their own house."
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law. They have expanded significantly under the current government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ultranationalist coalition partners, who critics accuse of giving tacit approval to settler violence.
One of Ridi's first acts after returning to Qusra was to fly an American flag from the roof of his building. He's asked the U.S. Embassy for help.
Qusra is about 16 kilometres south of Nablus as the crow flies and is surrounded by settlement blocs, including Migdalim and Shilo, as well as a growing number of outposts occupied by radical settlers.
Settler attacks causing casualties or property damage are averaging about six incidents a day this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — "higher than in any year on record."
The violence in Qusra prompted a rebuke from the U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who denounced those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" on social media.
"We're appalled at some of the things that have happened to families who are the victims of just criminal activity that is inexcusable and repugnant," he told Reuters in a later televised interview.
"I don't call them settlers," he said. "They're un-settlers."
Huckabee is a strong supporter of Israel's settlement policy and of Jewish claims to a biblical right to the land, referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria.
More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem. Many live in large, long-established blocs, while others live in unauthorized outposts considered illegal even under Israeli law, at least on paper.
Huckabee has dismissed violent settlers as a small minority.
Critics say that ignores what they describe as a de-facto institutional annexation of the West Bank that increasingly relies on violence.
"I think Mr Huckabee is missing the main point," said Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, an Israeli NGO that monitors Israeli settlements.
"The problem is not the specific house in Qusra. The problem is the system which produces this type of violence," he said.
"The idea that Israel can rule three million Palestinians in the West Bank through its military while more and more land is being grabbed and given to Israeli settlers."
At Qusra, Israeli border police and units from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) were deployed. The IDF said the forces were deployed to restore order and remove settlers blockading the Palestinian homes.

items.title: How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?
items.summary: Many questions have already been asked about the couple's return — but after being away for years following a tumultuous relationship with the British press that appeared to have been a factor in their decamping to California, could the tabloids' fascination about the couple peter out this time?
items.body_text:
How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?
The couple’s return comes amid questions about British media’s treatment of Black public figures
When Prince Harry and Meghan Markle return to Britain this month, they will be stepping back into a country that has spent six years talking about them from afar.
Their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are due to attend school in Britain in September, and the couple are expected to live privately outside London for an extended period, according to reports. They will remain non-working royals.
Many questions have already been asked about the couple's return — but after being away for years following a tumultuous relationship with the British press that appeared to have been a factor in their decamping to California, could the tabloids' fascination with the couple peter out this time?
Speculations about the life plans and movements of Royals are nothing new in Britain, but in the mythology that can sometimes be fomented around them, Harry and Meghan were often seen as "the evil, the bad cops, it's all very black and white," said Steven Barnett, a professor of communications at the University of Westminster.
"It's very binary.... There is a tendency in certain elements of the British press to go in for very personal witch hunts."
The early coverage included the Daily Mail's "(almost) straight outta Compton" headline about Meghan's mother and The Sun's "Harry's girl on Pornhub," which involved the tabloid discovering scenes from Markle's time on the American TV series Suits on a pornographic website, then apologizing for it months later.
A Guardian analysis of 843 articles across 14 U.K. newspapers from May 2018 to January 2020 found 43 per cent of coverage about Meghan was negative, compared with just eight per cent of 144 articles about Kate Middleton.
Royal commentator Afua Hagan said that interest would ramp up in Britain as they return.
She told Reuters while the couple were essentially walking back in to the "lion's den" they were better prepared this time: "They're not bringing a knife to a gunfight. They know what they have to do, what they're going to come up against, and will prepare themselves better."
It's not just the couple that has changed, Barnett said; "other soap operas" may be occupying the minds of the British public.
When Meghan and Harry first lived in the U.K., Barnett said, the country was in a different place.
"We didn't have, you know, two wars; the possibility of this country being drawn into a war with Russia; the ravages of climate change. Not to mention, cost of living problems and people struggling to get by."
Still, the court loss Prince Harry and several others recently suffered in privacy lawsuits they had filed against the Daily Mail could lead to more "nasty and vitriolic" coverage, Barnett said.
British media scrutinized after professor's death
The couple's return comes at a time of reckoning for British media.
The death this month of Jason Arday, a 41-year-old Cambridge professor who had resigned after allegations about his academic record, has prompted an intense debate over the boundaries of legitimate scrutiny — and whether the British press crossed them in its treatment of a Black public figure.
Some have made a connection between the nearly 250 articles that were published about Arday within two weeks, according to The Independent, and the negative coverage Markle received.
"The pile on that Meghan … got for years and years and years is akin to what Professor Jason Arday had. She was piled on for years and years and years and it still goes on," Nina Myskow, a former Sun columnist, said this week on Jeremy Vine, an eponymous chat show on Channel 5.
Barnett said the "personal assault" to which Arday was subjected was unfair, despite legitimate questions about plagiarism in his work and and Cambridge University's lack of vetting of it.

items.title: Zelenskyy vows response to deadly Russian multi-drone attack on shopping centre in central Ukraine
items.summary: At least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded on Friday when several Russian drones struck a ‌shopping centre in central Ukraine, authorities said, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy promising a response to what he called an "act of barbarism."
items.body_text:
Zelenskyy vows response to deadly Russian multi-drone attack on shopping centre in central Ukraine
Authorities say at least 16 dead, more than 130 wounded in daytime attack
At least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded on Friday when several Russian drones struck a shopping centre in central Ukraine, authorities said, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy promising a response to what he called an "act of barbarism."
Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that 22 children were among the wounded in the daytime attack on the city of Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelenskyy's hometown.
"There are 29 people in serious condition, including five children," Hanzha said. He posted a photo of black smoke billowing from a large industrial building.
In an update early on Saturday, Hanzha said nine people were preliminarily considered missing, including two children, and that rescuers were continuing to clear the rubble of the shopping centre.
Zelenskyy called the attack "absolutely cynical and despicable," saying that a second Russian drone hit the shopping centre half an hour after the first in what he said was a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.
'We will definitely respond'
"Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts," Zelenskyy said on Telegram, urging the world to hold Russia to account. "We will definitely respond."
In a post on X, Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief, said the shopping centre attack "shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow’s war."
"This is terror by design," Kallas said in the post. "Russia wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable."
Matthias Schmale, the UN humanitarian co-ordinator in Ukraine, condemned the deadly impact on civilians from Friday's attack in Kryvyi Rih.
"International humanitarian law prohibits indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian objects," Schmale said in a statement. "Civilians must be protected at all times."
In a separate attack on Friday, at least four people, including three children, were killed and a woman was wounded after a Russian drone strike in Ukraine's southern region of Mykolaiv, Ukrainian state media said on Telegram.
Russia is escalating its air war on Ukraine as fighting on the battlefield grinds toward the 4-1/2-year mark. On Thursday, 17 people were killed in a Russian ballistic missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.
Ukraine has also stepped up its own attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.
The two countries have been locked in a state of all-out conflict ever since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.
With files from CBC News

items.title: Retaliatory tariffs could be dangerous for both Canada and U.S., trade experts warn
items.summary: Collapse of trade talks did not surprise trade lawyers and experts watching the negotiations
items.body_text:
The collapse late Friday of the Canada-U.S. trade talks did not surprise trade lawyers and officials inside and beyond Canada, some of whom warned that escalating retaliatory tariffs could be highly damaging to both countries.
In an interview, Lawrence Herman, international trade lawyer at Herman & Associates in Toronto, said that he warned the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations last week that the talks probably would end in acrimony.
“Even with valiant efforts by Canadian negotiators being railroaded by the U.S. side, the real surprise would have been any deal that Canada could live with,” Mr. Herman said.
“Even then, we could have gotten an interim truce only, a short respite before being faced with a new set of Donald Trump diktats.”
After the talks went up in smoke, Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation on the new 50-per-cent tariffs imposed just after midnight on US$20-billion of Canadian exports on goods ranging from plywood and cement to hockey sticks and wine.
On Saturday, Mr. Carney said Canada’s retaliatory measures will be revealed in the coming days and will take effect Sept. 8.
Some trade observers said this retaliation by both sides was inevitable.
“Canada told the Americans in advance that if these tariffs landed, it would stop negotiating and retaliate,” Barry Appleton, senior fellow at the Center for International Law at New York Law School, told the Associated Press. “The American trade representative said publicly he would not tolerate retaliation. Both sides have now committed themselves in public, which is how escalation stops being a choice.”
Read the latest on U.S.-Canada trade escalation
U.S. President Donald Trump is no stranger to escalation. In early 2025, he slapped 10-per-cent tariffs on China and then doubled them a month later. China retaliated, triggering a rapid tit-for-tat tariff war that saw the U.S. tariffs hit 125-per-cent. Shortly thereafter, most of the tariffs on both sides were paused or rolled back.
“Canada likely wanted further sector-specific relief than the U.S. was willing to offer, or Canada’s concessions did not go far enough,” Ryan Majerus, a partner at Atlanta’s King & Spalding law firm, told AP. “Either way, I think both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp. But if Canada has agreed to impose [retaliatory] tariffs, the off-ramp may be even harder to find.”
On X, James E. Thorne, chief market strategist at Canada’s Wellington-Altus, an investment dealer, said retaliation might be no-win strategy for Canada.
“Canada does not need another era of Pierre Elliott Trudeau-style progressive theatre,” he said. “[Retaliation] is not a strategy. It is an emotional response masquerading as economic policy. … Tariffs do not raise productivity. They do not attract investment, reduce regulatory costs or make Canadian business more competitive.”
Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic U.S. Senator for Minnesota, an Ontario-Manitoba border state whose economy is highly dependent on Canada, lashed out at Mr. Trump for imposing 50-per-cent tariffs on Canada.
“That means higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families. Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos,” she said on X.
The Trump-Carney spat and breakdown in trade talks were broadly covered in the European press, though the stories were short, not prominently played and generally devoid of comment. Transatlantic trade issues have largely dropped out of the European news cycle since the heated negotiations of 2025.
Last year’s EU-U.S. trade battle generally went in the U.S.’s favour. The EU offered tariff concessions to lock in a U.S. tariff ceiling and avoid a retaliatory trade war. The EU dropped most of its tariffs on U.S. goods and accepted 15-per-cent tariffs on most of its exports.

items.title: John Ivison: Things are about to get verrrrrry ugly
items.summary: The pain will be felt on both sides of the border
items.body_text:
John Ivison: Things are about to get verrrrrry ugly
The pain will be felt on both sides of the border
The main business of Canadian foreign policy for nearly 160 years has been to remain friendly with the United States, while maintaining a measure of self-respect.
According to Prime Minister Mark Carney, last minute changes to the prospective Canada-U.S. deal meant that his government couldn’t sign on and still retain its conception of itself as a proud, independent country.
Recommended Videos
In an ad hoc press conference on Saturday morning, Carney explained that he ordered his trade negotiators home after the U.S. side added changes that would have imposed unjustified tariffs and undermined Canadian sovereignty.
The auto industry north of the border was already at risk under the terms of the putative deal, which would have cut the current tariff level in half. But Carney said a late adjustment meant the American side wanted the deal applied only to cars and light trucks, not vehicles such as Ford’s F-series Super Duty line, which the company plans to make in Oakville, Ont., or GM’s Silverado, made in Oshawa.
That shift would have made production uneconomic over time, Carney said.
The Americans also added language that would have limited Canada’s ability to strike new international trade deals.
The prime minister was asked whether the late involvement of the U.S. Commerce Secretary, Howard Lutnick, reversed the progress all sides had claimed earlier in the week.
Carney would only say that there were differences inside the Trump administration that only emerged in the last few days.
Ottawa had been prepared to make concessions, dropping counter-tariffs on steel and aluminum provided the U.S. lower theirs to levels that would allow Canadian exports to be economic. Carney said he was prepared to encourage provinces to return U.S. alcohol to provincial liquor store shelves, and to take “administrative measures” to give more access to the dairy sector.
But, ultimately, “(the U.S.) asked too much and offered too little.”
The consequences are likely to be profound for all involved. The U.S. has already begun the process of imposing 50 percent tariffs on $28-billion of Canadian goods. Carney promised dollar-for-dollar retaliation and now Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, says the Americans are working on measures to respond to Canadian retaliation.
The impact on Canadian businesses will be felt immediately. Economist Trevor Tombe estimated up to 90,000 job losses, with the electronics, plastic and consumer goods industries hardest hit.
But the pain will be felt on both sides of the border. The absurdity is that Trump is stoking the very inflationary pressures that are partly responsible for the surging bond yields that are so concerning to him. Such is his vexation that he suggested that he may instruct the U.S. military to intervene in the bond crisis, though even for this president an order to bomb Wall Street might be considered as an overreaction.
When the details of Canada’s retaliation are announced next week, Trump will also come under pressure from the impacted businesses and members of Congress. The American side is unlikely to be as united as the justifiably aggrieved Canadians.
The vast majority of citizens here support Carney’s decision to stand fast in the face of a bad deal, according to recent opinion polling.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s response suggests he realizes many Canadians see the Trump administration’s trade policy as an extortion racket aimed at getting paid for doing nothing. He urged Canadians to stand united and placed the blame for threatening jobs firmly on the U.S. side.
 That was in stark contrast to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who expressed her disappointment that the agreement had fallen apart and urged Ottawa to restart negotiations, without mentioning Trump.
In the normal course of events, that would be good advice.

items.title: Michael Higgins: Just how bad was this deal?
items.summary: Mark Carney owes Canadian the full details of why he pulled out of trade agreement with Trump
items.body_text:
Michael Higgins: Just how bad was this deal?
Mark Carney owes Canadian the full details of why he pulled out of trade agreement with Trump
Prime Minister Mark Carney always said he would walk away from a bad deal and has now done so.
But as the prime minister urges us to rally round the flag — again — he also needs to give Canadians full details as to why the trade talks with the United States collapsed.
Recommended Videos
The Liberal government is pointing out that it was U.S. demands that led to the collapse of the latest round of trade talks. It may well be that it was the uncompromising American president and his negotiators who brought us to this point where we are about to engage in potentially catastrophic tit-for-tat tariffs.
But how exactly did we get here and why? How is it that Carney suspended trade talks after reports that we were close to a deal? It is not enough to point fingers. What Canadians need are the full details of what was being offered and why it was rejected.
In a late statement Friday night, the prime minister addressed none of those concerns.
“Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future. We will set our own course to keep building Canada strong for all,” said the prime minister in his statement.
In a press conference Saturday, he repeatedly made the same refrain.
“We can’t control the storm that blows in from Washington,” he said in his introductory remarks. “We can, however, chart a new course by building Canada strong at home and diversifying our trading relationships abroad.
“We are masters in our own home and an excellent partner abroad.”
He later said, “Canadians will always take care of each other. We know we’re stronger together. In the last year and a half, Canadians have met this moment with resolve, with purpose, with strength.”
So here we are, back in Elbows Up territory. At least one good thing to come out of this trade war is that it will unite a majority of the country.

In his statement and his press conference, Carney said he decided to walk away from the trade negotiations because of unrealistic demands by the Americans.
“There were some things we wouldn’t do. We were not prepared to compromise Canada’s sovereignty or to undermine our key industries. We were not prepared to accept any compromise on our sovereignty, protection of the French language and our culture,” he said.
When pressed on specifics, Carney gave a few examples of friction between negotiators.
One was the auto sector. Earlier this week, the CBC reported that the U.S. was considering reducing auto tariffs down from 25 per cent to 15 per cent. But Carney said the U.S. wanted to limit the level of tariffs to cars only and exclude medium and heavy autos and light trucks. This would have made Canadian production “uneconomic,” he said.
Another major sticking point, said Carney, was the U.S. introducing at the last minute language that would have restricted Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries.
That was simply “unacceptable,” said the prime minister.
A third example, said Carney, was that the U.S. made “efforts to restrict our protections of our language, our culture, and in effect, our sovereignty.” The prime minister did not clarify what those efforts were or provide specifics details.
“In short, they asked too much and they offered too little,” said Carney.
Not surprisingly, the U.S. blamed Canada for the collapse of the talks.
The New York Times quoted U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer as saying, “Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week, despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market.

items.title: Carson Jerema: Mark Carney’s path from here is surprisingly obvious
items.summary: The end of free trade is a tragedy the Liberals failed to prepare for
items.body_text:
Carson Jerema: Mark Carney's path from here is surprisingly obvious
The end of free trade is a tragedy the Liberals failed to prepare for
If you need to blame Prime Minister Mark Carney for anything, be it for overpromising on his ability to get anything resembling an acceptable “deal” with U.S. President Donald Trump on trade, but his decision to walk away from negotiations Friday, based on what we know, was the right thing to do.
Leaked details of the tentative agreement that was reached earlier this week were bad enough. Apparently, according to media reports, Canada was conceding to permanent unilateral tariffs from the Americans on steel and autos, albeit at lower rates, while this country was expected to lift all tariffs, and make several non-trade concessions. These included scuppering digital legislation, a promise to complete the F-35 purchase and altering Canada’s supply management regime. Whatever one thinks of those policies, whether they are good or bad, they should be the purview of Ottawa, not Washington.
Recommended Videos
The fact that Canada was expected to make all these concessions while American tariffs remained in place is ludicrous. Not to mention that this little side deal already contravenes the existing Canada U.S. Mexico Agreement, which is somehow supposed to be renegotiated at some point.
Now we know that the deal on the table was evidently worse or became worse, than even all that. The Americans, according to Carney on Saturday morning, wanted to not only keep some tariffs on the auto sector, they wanted to exclude medium and heavy duty trucks from the deal altogether. Most galling of all, again, assuming the prime minister’s characterization of events is accurate, is that the U.S. wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to sign trade deals with other countries.
In other words, the plan was to turn Canada into a Western version of Belarus, where it is nominally independent but controlled from a foreign capital. Incidentally, what the Americans seem to want Canada to give up is not much different from what would have to be conceded if we joined the European Union, where Ottawa would also be prevented from signing independent trade deals and expected to align its regulatory regime with other members.
So walking away from negotiations, even if it leads to a protracted trade war, was the right thing to do. It may have been the most important moment for Canadian sovereignty in generations, and much credit to the prime minister for having the nerve to stand up.
-   Carson Jerema: Trump wants trade — just not on terms anyone can decipher
-   Jesse Kline: Deal or no deal, Carney Liberals have failed to build Canada

That said, the fact the Liberals benefit politically from conflict with Trump is notable, and eventually Carney will have to account for any prolonged economic pain that might result from this.
The larger challenge now is reversing decisions taken in Canada over decades that have made it uniquely vulnerable to the treatment it is currently facing from Trump. Living next to the most powerful and richest nation in history, which was somehow uniquely benign, and, until now, largely friendly, allowed successive politicians the luxury to delude themselves into thinking Canada was morally superior. The U.S. spends money on the military and is the home of ravenous capitalism, while Canada is a nation of health care, peacekeepers and multiculturalism.
This country’s entire national mythos since the 1960s has only been possible because the Americans had not been a genuine military threat since at least the Civil War, and possibly not since the War of 1812.
Additionally, given how wealthy the U.S. is, there has never been much pressure on Canada to ensure it is a business friendly country.
