items.title: Pope at Mass in Rimini: ‘At every level, authority is service'
items.summary: During the Mass concluding his one-day pastoral visit to San Marino and Rimini, Pope Leo XIV reminds the faithful that St. Peter’s faith is the foundation of our call to our call to service, following in the footsteps of Jesus, the Messiah, who became incarnate to serve humanity. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope at Mass in Rimini: âAt every level, authority is service'
By Christopher Wells
Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass for the Twenty-first Sunday of Ordinary Time at the Italian port of Rimini on Saturday evening, concluding a one-day pastoral visit that began in the Republic of San Marino and included an encounter with the participants in the âMeeting for Friendship Among Peoples.â
The Holy Father began his homily by recalling St. Peterâs profession of faith in Jesus as the Christ, the Messiah, recounted in the dayâs Gospel.
âWe are here,â Pope Leo said, âbecause we believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the eternal Son of the Father, consecrated and sent into the world âto serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.â
In Peterâs words, he continued, âwe recognize the truth that fills us with joy and hope, and we find the path that leads to life: the path of God who places Himself at the service of humanity.â
Pope Leo explained that this is how we should understand Jesusâ handing of the keys of the Kingdom, a gesture that shows us that in the Church, authority is service.
Not only bishops and priests, but every baptized person, he said, is called to embrace, reunite, welcome, liberate, forgive, and emancipate âanyone imprisoned by sin and its consequences.
Turning to the Old Testament reading, which saw the unjust steward removed from his position in favour of the righteous Eliakim, Pope Leo drew the lesson: âeverything we have and are is a gift from God to us, so that, in His hands, we can be instruments of salvation for one another in justice.â
Pope Leo went on to explain the âinscrutabilityâ of Godâs plans for usâexpressed by St Paul in the Second Readingâsaying that those plans are not complex because of the reasoning behind them, but because of âthe disarming immensity of His love, which surpasses all our capacity and expectations.â
This divine loved, which we are called to imitate, is mirrored in the honesty, generosity, and, benevolence of the people of the Romagna region, the Holy Father sad, as he encouraged them to continue to ensure that the area is welcoming, ânot only for its refreshment and entertainment, but also for its spirituality.â
In the context of the summer vacation that is drawing to a close, Pope Leo warned the faithful not to allow a period of rest to lead to âdispersion and ruin,â but rather to take the opportunity to find rest in a genuine encounter with God and other people in the depths of our souls.
He said the Christian community is called to foster this experience, as individuals and institutions, through hospitality, recollection, and the willingness âto help and to offer charity.â This applies not only to our engagement with those seeking rest and refreshment, but also with those âwounded in body and spirit, who seek refuge, food, and assistance far from their homeland.â
Quoting the local Bishop, Pope Leo XIV invited the faithful gathered for the Holy Mass to take up the attitudes of prayer, unity, listening, courage, simplicity, gratitude, before thanking them for their welcome and commending them to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary and their patron saints.

items.title: Pope meets with the sick and poor in Rimini: ‘You are home’
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV meets with people who are sick, persons with disabilities and people living in poverty assisted by Caritas in the Rimini Cathedral and reminds them of God’s love for them. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope meets with the sick and poor in Rimini: âYou are homeâ
By Kielce Gussie
After meeting those participating in the 47th Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Pope Leo XIV travelled to the Rimini Cathedral to meet with people who are sick, persons with disabilities and people living in poverty assisted by Caritas.
Expressing his gratitude for the Meeting, the Pope explained that the Cathedral is where âyou are at homeâ because Jesus welcomed the sick, the poor, and those with disabilities at the center to âheal them and restore to them a life worthy of their dignity.â
In that way, he demonstrated Godâs love and infinite mercy. After experiencing those signs and being healed, these people followed Jesus and joined his community of disciples.
Pope Leo urged everyone to follow this example. We are called to let Jesus heal us, to forgive us, and transform us. After that, we are called to walk together in his Church, that is the community he created to bring the Gospel to everyone.
With that in mind, the Pope once again thanked and encouraged everyone to âfollow the Lord by taking an active part in the life of the Churchâin the parish, in associations, and in places of welcome and service.â It is in these moments that we learn and experience Godâs great love and realize that we are all his children and brothers and sisters to one another.
The Diocesan Caritas of Rimini offers a variety of services to help and care for the most vulnerable people in the local community. Some of the initiatives include a soup kitchen, Grandparentsâ Outreach Service, prison services, and street outreach.
Supporting the Popeâs Mission
In his welcoming address to the Pope, Bishop Nicolò Anselmi recalled the figures who inspire the Diocese spiritually: from the two young people recently beatified, Sandra Sabattini and Alberto Marvelli, to the witness of the Servant of God Fr. Oreste Benzi, a priest from Rimini and founder of the Pope John XXIII Community. They are an inspiration to so many of the brothers and sisters present, âwho are going through a difficult period in their livesâ: from illness to addiction, as well as imprisonment. âJesus is asking you to care for these people,â the bishop said.
Bishop Anselmi explained to Pope Leo that the cathedral houses two important relics: one of Saint Nicholas of Bari, âwhich offers us the opportunity to engage in ongoing ecumenical dialogue,â and a cloth bearing the blood of Saint John Paul II, âdisplayed here in an exhibition that includes a photograph of Pope WojtyÅa alongside a very young Robert Prevost.â
Finally, the bishop addressed the Pope with words of trust and commitment: âWe want to help you carry out this great task. We too, with you and like Peter, want Jesus and want to love one another. Bless us, Your Holiness, in this desire for love that we wish to live in our families, in our diocese and in the world.â

items.title: The Hour of Responsibility
items.summary: The words of Pope Leo XIV at the Meeting in Rimini and his call for the authentic realism of mercy against the false realism that would have us rearm Read all
items.body_text:
The Hour of Responsibility
By Andrea Tornielli
âAgainst the false realism that rearms minds, words, and nations, Catholic culture today must set the realism of mercy, in which there can be no enemies, and all people, even adversaries, are brothers and sisters to be looked in the eye and encountered in truth.â
These are the words Pope Leo XIV addressed to the participants at the Meeting in Rimini, and in particular to the thousands of young people who bring the great end-of-summer gathering to life, a gathering that grew out of the experience of Communion and Liberation. They were not words spoken merely for the occasion, but a precise invitation. First and foremost, an invitation to look at the reality in which we are living.
Already 44 years ago, Saint John Paul II, speaking at the Meeting, had emphasized the beauty of words such as âencounterâ and âfriendship among peoplesâ during what he himself called âdramatic moments in the history of the world.â
Today, the international situation is even more uncertain and precarious than it was then: a growing number of conflicts, ongoing massacres of civilians and childrenâone need only think of Gaza and Ukraineâand the many nations investing ever greater sums in rearming themselves. Faced with all this, the Pope recalls the vocation of the Meeting, which is not to be âa sort of enclave,â but a âcrossroadsâ of encounters and dialogue.
This, Pope Leo said, is the hour of responsibility.
To follow Christ today, after the tragedies of the twentieth century, means fully recognizing that evil cannot be fought with evil. The only answer, the Christian answer, is loveââthe method of redemption,â embodied by the crucified Messiah. And so, to those who today, in the name of a presumed realismâwhich the Pope did not hesitate to call âfalseââwould rearm minds, words and nations, Catholic culture responds with an authentic realism: the realism of mercy, âin which there can be no enemies, and all people, even adversaries, are brothers and sisters to be looked in the eye and encountered in truth.â
There is therefore a need for courageous pioneers who will commit themselves concretely to freeing human coexistence from suspicion, work from the idolatry of profit, and technology and finance from the business of death.
Pope Leo calls for the exposure of âunjust power relationsâ that lie âat the root of poverty and inequality, war and environmental disasters.â This is a strong and consequential appeal from the Successor of Peter, who from the very first day of his pontificate has spoken of âunarmed and disarmingâ peace, and it should be kept in mind as a criterion for judging the social and even political engagement of all Catholic laypeople.
It is also particularly significant that the Pope invites the people of the Meeting to take risks, to put themselves on the line, âbroadening their bonds beyond every overly narrow sense of belonging.â For the Communion and Liberation Movement, groups and communities must become a springboard for diving into the whole of reality, resisting whatever would seek to distance them from brothers and sisters of different cultures, sensibilities and backgrounds, âespecially the poorest.â
Finally, it is worth emphasizing the Popeâs reminder that there is never coercion, indoctrination or recruitment in love, because there is love only in freedom, in living encounter and in the generous gift of oneself.

items.title: Cardinal Brislin joins African clergy in calling Israel’s actions in Gaza genocide
items.summary: VATICAN CITY (RNS) — Drawing on Africa’s experience of apartheid, genocide and war, Cardinal Stephen Brislin and nine other Catholic clergy say Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide — and argue silence is no longer an option.
items.body_text:
Cardinal Brislin joins African clergy in calling Israel’s actions in Gaza genocide
VATICAN CITY (RNS) – Ten Catholic clergy from Africa, including Cardinal Stephen Brislin of South Africa, issued a statement Friday (Aug. 21) describing the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza as genocide, drawing on their continent’s experience of war and apartheid.
“We believe that the policies and actions of the Government of Israel in Gaza constitute genocide,” the statement read, citing arguments by international legal scholars and genocide experts. “Having learned to recognise dehumanisation in our own history, we cannot refuse to recognise it in another people.”
The statement was issued by Priests Against Genocide, a network of Catholic priests, bishops and cardinals advocating for Palestinian rights. The organization was founded in 2025 and says it represents over 2,500 members across 67 countries.
On Sunday, Pope Leo made an appeal for peace and called for a two-state solution that would respect the national integrity of Israel and Palestine. But the pontiff has stopped short of declaring Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide.
Brislin, among the signatories of the statement, is the Archbishop of Johannesburg in South Africa and was appointed last year by Pope Leo as a member of the Vatican department overseeing clergy. The pope also gave Breslin a prominent advisory role in the June consistory, a summit of cardinals.
South Africa — which enforced racial segregation and white minority rule, called apartheid, between 1948 and 1994 — has a long history of Palestinian advocacy. Nelson Mandela, the anti-apartheid leader who became the country’s first Black president, declared in 1997 that “our freedom is incomplete without the freedom of the Palestinians.”
In December 2023, South Africa brought a case before the International Court of Justice accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in its war in Gaza. South Africa argued that Israel’s conduct unfolded “against a background of apartheid” and an “institutionalized regime of discriminatory laws, policies and practices” toward Palestinians. The case is still pending with the ICJ.
In their statement, the African clergy said they “cannot condemn apartheid in our history and refuse to recognise these patterns inflicted upon Palestinians.”
The statement, directly addressed to the government of Israel, also rejected “antisemitism and Islamophobia alike” and condemned the “grave crimes” committed by Hamas on Oct 7, 2023, that resulted in the death of about 1,200 people in Israel and the abduction of some 250 hostages.
“Their crimes do not diminish Israel’s obligations under international law, nor justify genocide or collective punishment. We will not answer one dehumanisation with another,” the statement added.
Israel has not issued a response to the clergy’s statement but has denied past genocide allegations, stating that its war is against Hamas and not Palestinians.
Israel launched its military offensive in Gaza after the Oct 7. attack. Since then, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory’s Health Ministry, including at least 21,000 children. A ceasefire took effect on October of last year, but Israeli strikes and gunfire have continued, killing more than 1,200 Palestinians since the agreement. Tensions have also intensified in the occupied West Bank as attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians have increased.
Friday’s statement called for Israel to put an immediate end to “genocidal policies” and forced displacement and to cooperate with international judicial systems. The signatories also asked that Israel suspend weapons and technologies that risk violating international law. And they called on Christian groups to scrutinize their investments for ties to human rights violations. items.title: Christian nationalists’ professed support for religious pluralism is often drowned out by perceptions that Christians are under threat
items.summary: (The Conversation) — Two political scientists explain why Christian nationalist beliefs endure.
items.body_text:
Christian nationalists’ professed support for religious pluralism is often drowned out by perceptions that Christians are under threat
(The Conversation) — Christian nationalism, a worldview that sees the United States as a Christian nation and believes that Christianity should have a privileged role in American civic life, has been shown to be related to a host of social attitudes.
Research shows that people who hold Christian nationalistic beliefs tend to, on average, also show antipathy toward religious minorities and racial and ethnic minorities, as well as have sexist and anti-democratic attitudes.
Our research found that many Christian nationalists endorse religious pluralism, meaning that they value religious diversity – in principle. But we also found that this support for religious pluralism is often drowned out by perceptions of threats to Christians.
How we did the research
For our new research, published in the academic journal Politics & Religion in March 2026, we surveyed 1,500 American Christians in January 2024.
In healthy democracies, most citizens respect the civil liberties of others, including members of social groups they dislike. We asked our respondents which social group they liked the least, such as Christian fundamentalists, environmental activists, President Donald Trump supporters or atheists. We then asked them if they thought members of that group should be able to make public speeches, teach in public schools or run for political office, among others. The responses, taken together, showed respondents’ political tolerance for people who they dislike.
We also asked respondents how much they agreed with a series of statements commonly used to measure support for Christian nationalism, such as whether the federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation. On a scale of 0 to 1, the average Christian nationalism score was 0.64, indicating that American Christians tend to support the idea of a Christian America.
To capture ideas that run directly counter to Christian nationalism, we then asked about their support for religious pluralism. Respondents agreed or disagreed with statements such as “nations should not favor one religion over another,” and “we need to advocate the Christian values of loving your neighbor as yourself.” Together, these made up our anti-Christian nationalism measure.
On average, participants rated their agreement with these statements as 0.74, higher than the agreement with Christian nationalist ideas – suggesting that anti-Christian nationalist views were more widely supported by American Christians.
What the research found
Some of the survey questions measuring Christian nationalism and anti-Christian nationalism captured opposite ideas.
Without assigning respondents to any categories, we asked them if they agreed with statements like “The federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation” or “Nations should not favor one religion over another.” We found that people who agreed with one were likely to agree with the other. In other words, respondents who advocated for a Christian nation also affirmed religious freedom for all.
While this might seem surprising, social scientists have long known that people hold lots of conflicting arguments in their heads. American Christians have likely heard both Christian nationalist and anti-Christian nationalist messages through their congregations, media and social networks.
Our statistical models show that religious pluralism is related to tolerance differently depending on views on Christian nationalism. We isolated strong supporters and strong opponents of Christian nationalism. Predictably, among strong opponents of Christian nationalism, anti-Christian nationalism views were associated with increased tolerance. But, surprisingly, strong supporters of Christian nationalism maintained the same level of tolerance.

items.title: Once shaped by court rituals, China’s imperial cuisine lives on today
items.summary: BEIJING (AP) — Imperial cuisine encompasses the meals emperors ate daily and the feasts their courts held throughout the year.
items.body_text:
Once shaped by court rituals, China’s imperial cuisine lives on today
BEIJING (AP) — It is said that Empress Dowager Cixi once dreamed of a pastry during the final decades of imperial China.
The same treat was served to her at breakfast the following morning. Delighted, she summoned her chef and rewarded him with a silver ingot.
“It was originally called ‘minced pork pancake,’ but because it had fulfilled her dream, it later became known as ‘dream pastry,’” said Zhou Tong, a chef at Fangshan Restaurant in Beijing.
Fangshan specializes in imperial cuisine, preserving dishes like the one associated with Cixi and other culinary traditions from China’s imperial court. The restaurant was founded in 1925 by former chefs from the Qing Dynasty at Beihai Park, a garden where royals from several dynasties rested, handled government affairs and performed ritual sacrifices.
“The name Fangshan literally means ‘imitating the imperial cuisine,’” said assistant general manager Di Xin.
A handful of other Beijing restaurants also serve versions of imperial cuisine, while the Palace Museum preserves Qing-dynasty objects tied to court dining, including pastry molds.
Every meal comes with its own rules
Imperial cuisine encompasses the meals emperors ate daily and the feasts their courts held throughout the year.
Each had its own rituals. Drinking milk tea, for instance, was an important first step at Qing-dynasty banquets, said Teng Deyong, a researcher at China’s Palace Museum.
During the banquet, the emperor bestowed wine or food on princes and officials. Recipients performed rites and paid their respects to him before they ate or drank.
Aside from banquets, sacrificial rituals were held. They followed a separate system and could involve meat offerings.
“At the Palace of Earthly Tranquillity, there was the eating of sacrificial pork, which we know was one of the most important rituals of the Qing imperial court,” Teng said.
In that ritual, fatty pork was boiled without salt. After the ceremony, it was distributed among guests, and receiving the sacrificial meat was considered a great honor.
Unseasoned food also appears in earlier Chinese ritual traditions. Wandi Wang, a professor of Chinese at Lehigh University in Pennsylvania, said the “Book of Rites,” a classical work on rites and ceremonies, describes a meat broth known as “grand stew” that was served without seasoning during sacrificial ceremonies.
“The absence of added flavoring was itself meaningful: the unseasoned dish evoked an earlier and simpler way of cooking and thus expressed a ritual ideal of honoring antiquity and remembering cultural origins,” Wang said.
Traditional techniques keep imperial pastry-making alive
Pastries were key to imperial cuisine, and the court had an institution specialized in making them.
Sweets made at Fangshan by Zhou include Cixi’s dream pastry and a small steamed corn bun. Their recipes are rooted in the imperial court.
“When customers visit, our servers often tell them the stories behind these dishes,” Zhou said. “People enjoy them even more because they carry such meaningful history.”
He learned his pastry-making technique from a master who had also learned from a mentor. It’s a craft that has been passed from one generation to the next.
Traditional imperial methods mean cooking must be done by hand — no blenders or food processors are allowed. Ingredients like beans are pulverized using sieves and certain flours are handled in custom-made copper pots.
“A machine may be more convenient, but the texture is completely different,” Zhou said. “You lose the delicate graininess and sandy mouthfeel that handcrafted pastries are supposed to have.”
Among Fangshan’s bestselling delicacies are the pea flour cake and the red bean roll. During the busy season, customers order more than 200 of the cakes per day.
